speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, April 19, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in this debate, I do so primarily as the elected representative of the Rosthern constituency, but I believe I am correct in saying that we are all elected to this democratic parliament to look after the interests of the people in all parts of Canada.
It is a privilege and a pleasure to open my address by extending warm congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) upon his great effort this year. I believe there is no more arduous position in the government of our great country than the one which he holds. I feel sure that the people of Canada, irrespective of party, appreciate the services that he has given to our country. It is quite generally known that he has served us in this difficult task at great financial sacrifice. To unthinking people who cynically criticize politicians I would throw out this challenge. Let anyone who belittles the services of those who guide our political destinies show where they have made comparable sacrifices in seeking to serve other than their personal interests. It is my hope, and I believe it is the hope of a large number of Canadians, that the Minister of Finance,

The Budget-Mr. Boucher during the critical period through which we are passing, will remain in the office he now holds.
It is a pleasure to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Prudham) on his elevation to the cabinet as Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. The minister, at a comparatively early age, has made a success of his private business, and I am confident he will extend his record of success as he continues to serve his country in public life. We of his neighbouring province of Saskatchewan will watch his career with a great deal of interest and enthusiasm.
I know that no minister and no government is happy when it becomes necessary to increase the taxes which they must collect to administer the affairs of the country. I feel sure, however, that our people will understand and appreciate the need for a greater contribution at this time. A large proportion of the people of Saskatchewan have come from the countries of central Europe. They came to Canada to escape wars and rumours of wars. They know, even better than we know, that the security of our nation, the security of our homes, is a primary need if we are to build a community of prosperous and happy people. For this reason I am sure that each person in Canada will consider it a privilege to bear his share of the cost of protecting our homes from invasion by the communists.
I take second place to no one in advocating the greatest possible measures of social security. But all our security measures would be worthless if we neglected our defences and let ourselves be overcome by the aggressive communist forces in the world. We would be enslaved without recourse. It is for this reason, then, that I am particularly proud to support a government that has given so much of its energy and ability, especially in the last year, to the preservation of peace. One of the greatest guarantees that we can have for peace is to remain united and strong with our western neighbours. The record of the government of Canada in its quest for peace is a notable one, which needs and deserves the support of all peace-loving people. We were proud to see our own minister of external affairs appointed to the cease-fire committee of the United Nations. His efforts were tireless, and I feel sure that they will yet have an important effect, even if it is not obvious at this time.
The efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and of the government as a whole to preserve peace have been a sharp blow to the aggressive forces of the world which use the language of peace in order to


weaken the free nations and leave them prey to the aggressive intentions of Russian imperialism. The quest for peace and the necessary action to defend our homes against communist aggression must come first in all our plans and expenditures, because these things are basic in our search for prosperity and happiness.
An important part of these basic aims includes certain developments at home to increase our production. I refer particularly to the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project. This project will give stability to a large section of our productive prairie land, in addition to the production from the lands which are actually irrigated. The early completion of this project will enable us to make a greater contribution to our national and humanitarian desires.
During this session we have had the interesting spectacle of an opposition which has spoken, and continues to speak, with two voices on the question of the special powers to be given our government to be used as and when needed to protect our homes. On the one hand the opposition has used extreme statements in accusing the government of trying to take undemocratic powers, while on the other hand it has criticized the government severely because the government does not use special powers more drastically. In my constituency, and in the province of Saskatchewan generally, I have found that the majority of the people trust this government to use special powers with the greatest discretion and in the interests of all our people.
The farmers of my constituency-and practically all our people, because we all live directly or indirectly from our farms-are enthusiastic supporters of the wheat board. I regret to say that the socialist government of Saskatchewan has done our farmers a great disservice by sniping continuously at the work of the board in an effort to make political capital for itself. It has thus given aid and comfort to those who are trying to break this method of marketing and to bring back the open market of the Winnipeg grain exchange. I believe our farmers will remain steadfast in support of the wheat board. They have a great fear of what could happen to them, with so much frozen and low-grade grain, if they were thrown on the mercy of the Winnipeg grain exchange or any other open market. They know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) have not let them down, and I am sure that they will refuse to be stampeded into any position that will threaten the continuance of

the wheat board and the pooling system of handling and selling their grain.

I now wish to say a word about the report of the royal commission on transportation. I want to congratulate the royal commission on transportation on the thoroughness with which they have made the investigation assigned to them by this government. The implementation of this report will go a long way toward overcoming many of the inequities that have existed in the economy of the widely separated areas of Canada, and I would strongly recommend that this report be implemented as soon as possible. I am pleased and proud, Mr. Speaker, that my predecessor, Mr. Walter Tucker, gets credit for the great contribution he made to this matter. Over the past few years there has been overtaxation year by year. Finally, measures should be taken to meet the high cost of living arising from profiteering.
This has been a most unreal discussion. All the statements made by the hon. member for Greenwood, and offered as his considered criticism, have been unanswered by any member of the government. Never before in my experience in the house has the government of the day been unable to answer criticisms and has therefore remained silent, as this government has in recent days. It is all very well for the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Boucher) to say that everyone is satisfied-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before dealing in general with some matters that I should like to discuss-because the budget gives to members an opportunity of bringing to the attention of the government matters of interest to their constituents and to the people of the country as a whole-I should like to refer once more to the serious situation on the prairies resulting from a lack of the necessary freight cars to move the wheat crop, amounting to tens of millions of bushels. That problem is not answered by statistics given by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). It is one that affects every farmer in western Canada. Having regard to the conditions which prevailed last fall, many millions of bushels of wheat are in danger of being lost entirely as a result of failure to act on the question of the supply of freight cars.
There will be serious loss to farmers everywhere unless something is done about it.
It is all very well to say that there are not as many freight cars in the United States now as there were three, four or five weeks ago, but the adverse balance of freight cars in the United States today is still a great deal more than one and a half times what it normally has been in past years. Nothing has been done about it except consultation. I mentioned the other day, and I repeat, that in 1919 a similar condition existed, and the then government of Canada appealed to the government of the United States to do something. Even today, with the month of April almost gone, I urge the government to make
20. 1951
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker representations to the government of the United States to the end that something be done in this regard; otherwise something approaching disaster faces western farmers.
I hold in my hand a resolution dated April 16, which comes from a town in Saskatchewan with a population of about 400. It states that the elevators are filled; 410,000 bushels of grain are in the elevators, but there are an estimated 200,000 bushels among the farmers that cannot be disposed of, part of which is wet wheat or damp wheat. I am not one of those who over the years has believed in bringing up only such matters as are of particular interest to my own area; this is a condition which prevails, and I make an appeal that something be done before it is too late.
In view of the situation which now exists, most farmers will have to face the necessity of providing their own storage. I therefore suggest that consideration be given, as has been done in the United States, to adequate balance of payments for farm storage so that the farmers themselves will be in a position to arrange for a type of storage which will meet present needs.
The quota system has been unfair and inequitable, and the result is that in certain areas only a portion, and not a large portion, of the crop of last year has been sold. I ask the government to act immediately, and not merely by a parade of statistics. The situation is serious when one considers that 170 million bushels of wheat are unsold in the western provinces.
I now wish to say a few words about the budget. Last fall I had the honour, along with other hon. members, of attending the meetings of the commonwealth parliamentary association in New Zealand and Australia, and in passing I would pay my tribute to the bountiful hospitality and warm welcome extended to us by the governments of these two commonwealth countries. It was pointed out by one after another of the representatives there that one of the greatest allies that Stalin has in the world today is inflation. The Minister of Finance said in his address the other night that inflation was more serious in Australia than it is in Canada. That was not my view while I was there. In Canada there is almost hysterical inflation, mounting from day to day to an extent never before equalled, and with no effective action being taken by the government. The leader of the opposition referred to the condition as runaway inflation; I think it is actually galloping inflation. Nothing in particular is being done to meet the problem of the ever-declining savings measured in purchasing power of our people, those who invested their money in

The Budget-Mr. Diefenhaker insurance, those who are in receipt of pensions. Inflation has cut away almost half of the purchasing power of their savings or allowances. Great as are hidden taxes, the most objectionable of all is inflation. It undermines and destroys. Burglary is an offence; but the silent, effective theft of inflation undermines the fabric of our country-and no effective action is taken.
The situation is so serious as to merit something more than adulation of the government as exemplified by some hon. members. That provides no remedy. None of us wants a condition such as this to continue, and when there are criticisms it is because we believe they are called for in view of the gravity of the situation as we see it.
The Minister of Finance contended that the extra levy of sales tax really did not amount to anything for persons in the lower income brackets for it covers only about twenty-five per cent of the commodities purchased by those whose incomes are less than $3,000. But that is not the whole story. There is no tax on bread; yet the sales tax actually increases the price of bread to the consumer. Sales tax is imposed on the motor vehicles used for delivery, on the wrappings of the bread, on the machinery and equipment that goes into the production of bread, and so forth.
Hidden taxation is greater than ever before in our history, and it is being increased at a time when inflation is at its height. There can be no answer to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Greenwood that the increasing of the sales tax would increase prices. It has done so already. While we talk of its effects, prices rise on commodities subject to the additional sales tax.
Only in the last few days the prices of cigarettes and gasoline have been increased, and there is also the expected increase in the price of oil used for agricultural purposes. Prices of furniture and shoes are rising at a time when the government should act to meet the situation relative to inflation.
One of the means suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood was that there should be a reduction in government expenditures. The answer of the minister is: There was; we have attacked the problem. Well, of $1,992 million of non-defence expenditures the reduction has been $35 million, or just one and four-fifths cents on the dollar.
Why could not the government set up a commission similar to that advocated last year by the leader of the opposition, similar to the Hoover commission in the United States, which recommended savings of hundreds of millions of dollars in controllable
expenditures? Why could this not be done, at a time when it is so necessary in the preparation of our defences?
If we do not win the fight against inflation, defence costs will mount to intolerable and bankrupting heights. We cannot beat Stalin with a 56-cent dollar and maintain incentive in our country. The other day the Minister of Finance, in clarion tones, called for action to meet inflation. But a few minutes later his voice was muffled by its own inconsistency when living costs were increased to every family in the country by the increase of the general sales tax to the extent of twenty-five per cent.
If the government had practised economy the extra sales tax would not have been necessary. I agree with the subamendment of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) wherein he suggests that the incomes of single persons earning up to $1,500 and married persons earning up to $3,000 should be exempt from the defence surtax. I think there is justification for that position.
Exemption from personal income tax is based upon the considered opinion of government authorities as to what it costs the individual or the ordinary family to live. But when provision was made for the present exemption, on March 22, 1949, the cost of living index stood at 159-5, whereas today it is 179-5, representing an increase of about twenty-one per cent. In view of the statistics set forth in the Labour Gazette of March 1951, unless the standard of living of persons in low income tax brackets is to be materially reduced there must be an increase in the amount of exemptions.
Having said that, I am not going to indulge in any further criticism of the budget. The Minister of Finance said the other night in a radio speech that he thought the people were satisfied with it. That has not been my experience. I know of no family in this country in the lower income brackets that can find justification for the imposition of an additional sales tax at a time when they find it almost impossible to carry on by reason of the increased cost of living.
We need money to finance the country; that was admitted by the hon. member for Greenwood, Yes, we must meet the danger we face throughout the world, and we can meet it with an economy-minded government that will scrupulously reduce all unnecessary expenditures. What have they done? The Minister of Finance in his radio speech said in effect: Did we not reduce the number of civil servants by five per cent? When he says that, I think of the mail carriers in

various parts of the country, overworked as they were before the reduction; I think of the paltry savings effected by their removal from office and I have a suspicion that the mail carrier was chosen so that in every community the people would see at first hand that something was being done by the government to economize. In the face of reductions that could be made, and in the light of what the Hoover commission in the United States showed could be done and was done in that country, the interference with the employment of these post office employees, hardworking as they are, is not justified on the grounds of economy or otherwise.
Yesterday over the air we listened to General MacArthur in one of the most outstanding speeches made anywhere in the world since last June when, for the first time the conscience of mankind moved against international wrongdoing.
Unfortunately within the last few weeks I have been obliged to be absent from the house for some time. But I have read Hansard more carefully, Mr Speaker, than I do even when I am here. One thing that strikes me particularly is that members of this house know so little about what the government proposes to do with reference to international affairs that affect the people of Canada. General MacArthur said much yesterday about the need of expanding the area of warfare in Korea to the Yalu river, and about the bombing of portions of China. I am not going to enter into any controversy on these matters; they are for military men. But in such a course there are dangers that are not attributable to appeasement.
At the commonwealth conference in New Zealand, and the later one in Australia, there were representatives of every colour and race from every part of the commonwealth, and there were among them some who spoke of the need of effectively using the atomic bomb against the North Koreans. I bring to you today, Mr. Speaker, the answer of the coloured races from every part of the world, from Asia, from Africa, from other areas in the south Pacific. Every one of the coloured races represented there argued against that. They said in effect: Do not discriminate against us again. Do not use the atomic bomb a third time against a coloured race, for in doing so you will unite the coloured races everywhere in the world against the white democratic peoples. That was their message, and it is a message that I believe deserves consideration.
Yesterday General MacArthur stated his position on Formosa, which he regards as
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker a bastion in the western Pacific. The attitude taken by the British government seems to be that, as Mr. Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill had made certain agreements at Cairo, those agreements should be carried out and Formosa turned over to China. I ask you, Mr. Speaker: Who in this house knows what the attitude of Canada is going to be on this matter so important to the future peace of the world? I feel that we have a right to ask that the fullest possible discussion take place on these matters in the House of Commons and not in the service clubs, that we in parliament have a right to know what our government will do on our behalf in a matter that affects the future of every Canadian and our very way of life.
What will be its attitude to Formosa with relation to the United Nations? What stand has the Canadian government taken with relation to the United Nations and expansion of the area of active warfare north of the boundaries of North Korea? These are matters the import of which concerns the salvation and future not only of people in other parts of the world but ourselves. I will give you the picture as I saw it in the commonwealth parliamentary association. There were representatives from the various provinces of the dominion. From this house there were the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford), the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Beaudoin), the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacNaught), the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), and we were accompanied by the Clerk of the House of Commons, Mr. Leon Raymond, K.C., O.B.E. Senator Roebuck represented the other place and was chosen as the chairman of the council.
We went over there to an unofficial parliament of representatives of every part of the commonwealth. I have heard Canadians say sometimes that there is no future for the British commonwealth. Such views were answered when one after the other these men representing every religion, race and colour spoke of what the British commonwealth meant and what it would mean to the future of the world and to freedom. I think of one representative from India who spent years fighting for his national freedom, and who measured his contribution in the biographical sketch in the back of the guide by the number of years that he had been in prison. He said to me one day: Do not sell the commonwealth short. Realize that it comprises 22 per cent of the world's population and does 33 per cent of the world's trade compared with 8 per cent on the part of the Soviet republic and all the

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker puppets aligned with it. Freedom depends on the survival of Britain and the commonwealth.
The strength and diversity of the commonwealth are things that we do not often speak about because for some reason it is not popular to do so. These men of every race and colour asked that we ensure within the commonwealth freedom from discrimination and thereby unite every part of the commonwealth against communism. None of them seemed to consider war inevitable; but the common feeling was that as communism advances in southeast Asia and gradually stretches its hand in the direction of Australia and New Zealand the commonwealth should stand together.
They pointed out that Singapore is weak compared to the days before the last war, that all through the Malayan states communism has infiltrated, that in Ceylon a very considerable percentage of the representation of their parliament is composed of communists. I do not presume to interfere with the internal affairs of other countries within the commonwealth but when one reads of the situation in South Africa it is very disturbing in a world where communism is doing its best to enlist the coloured races in its ranks on the promise of material advantage in return, coupled with equality without regard to race or colour.
I am convinced that wherever there is antiracialism or hunger exists there are potential breeding grounds of communism. It is for that reason that they asked, first, that each of the countries within the British commonwealth and empire eschew anything that discriminates against any race or colour. They contended too that in addition to military assistance we should do our part, not in a spirit of charity but in a spirit of Christian benevolence, to assist underprivileged peoples and thereby raise their living standards.
The other day I listened to the admirable address of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank), in which he left with the members of this house a message that could have come only from the heart. He asked for the support of the Colombo plan as a means to meet the advance of communism in Asia. Those who live in the Pacific area believe that the great danger spots of communist aggression are in Asia. The attitude taken in the United Kingdom is that the danger spot is in western Germany. I am speaking only of the Asiatic situation, for that was one about which we learned particularly at the time of that conference.

The yearnings of peoples suffering from hunger cannot be met by the promise of parliamentary government and democracy alone. H-bombs are not all we need fear in Asia. The H-weapon of communism is hunger. I am disappointed that Canada, having agreed to advance $25 million under the Colombo pact-a mere drop in the bucket when compared with the cost of our defence program -did not agree to send to India, at a time when 40 million people are facing starvation, the best wheat available in our country, rather than wheat that could not be milled. We should make a contribution to the welfare of the people of India now, when they need it. At the same time, if the matter is looked at from the national interest we would have been building up future markets; we would have been building up goodwill, and would have been meeting the onrush of communism which, as never before in history, challenges the future of democracy in Asia.
The representatives of various coloured races spoke English with faultless diction and with a power and eloquence that we whose native tongue is English seldom equal. These races are moved by resurgence of nationalistic pride greater than at any time in history. They want freedom to preserve their fundamental rights, by way of democratic government. They want something that will meet their material demands. Communism promises an acre of land. We cannot do that but we can help to ease the gnawing pangs of ever-recurrent hunger. When Liaquat Ali Khan spoke in this house, I wondered what he meant when he said:
There can be no peace without removing the economic disequilibrium which keeps more than half the world in poverty and the ferment of discontent. Neither peace nor progress is possible without international co-operation.
I know now, and that is why I make this appeal. I ask the government of Canada to do something tangible in connection with the Colombo plan it has accepted before millions starve. How many of us realize that the population of the world is increasing at the rate of 60,000 a day? How many of us appreciate that if India were able to reduce her death toll by raising health standards and improving living standards, at the end of a hundred years its population would be twice the present population of the world? The increase in the world population is taking place mainly in Asia and Africa, and it is for that reason we must meet communism there. If it gains control there, world control will be an easier objective.
We have to break the stalemate of inflation which uncontrolled will emasculate our country and its efforts. At the same time

we have to accept our international responsibilities in connection with helping to raise the standards of underprivileged countries. As the leader of the opposition has said on more than one occasion, while plans to meet inflation give temporary relief, no final solution for the problem can be secured except by greater production. How are we going to get that? Some who attended the parliamentary conference spoke of Australia, of New Zealand and of Canada, great countries with tremendous resources still undeveloped. They contended that they should not be denied admission to these countries only because of their colour. They were perfectly willing to be denied admission on economic grounds and provided we had the necessary population and were developing our countries so that our greater production would help them and raise living standards elsewhere.
If we are to meet this problem of inflation- and I intend to deal with the question of immigration and will on another occasion, merely make this passing reference now-we will have to greatly increase our population within the next ten or fifteen years. Otherwise we will not be able to meet the demands that face us, nor will we be able to fulfil our responsibilities, having regard to the magnetic influence on communist peoples of a country with our vast resources. Last year 73,000 people came to Canada as immigrants, while 31,000 left Canada as emigrants. That shows that there is something wanting, something that has to be done. After all it does not mean very much to have an immigration policy under which two people are brought into our country while one Canadian leaves in the same period.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say we must meet the problem of inflation. We must do something more than bring forward statistics and say things are not as bad as they seem. Even at this time the government of this country would be doing something worth while if it were to agree to the setting up of a commission similar to the Hoover commission which did so much in the United States. For some reason or other, however, the government takes an adamant attitude toward this suggestion. In the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States members do not practise their political partisanship to the extent that one might imagine. There, in committee, without regard to party, considerable amounts were written off even the defence estimates without in any way diminishing the effectiveness of the national contribution. I feel this problem must be met, and it cannot be met by adding to the cost of living through taxation under a general sales tax, at a time when people
The Budget-Mr. Byrne already face the highest cost of living in history. I wonder what hon. gentlemen opposite would say if they were over here and a Conservative government were in power, with the cost of living higher than ever before. Surely, so far as our people in the low income brackets are concerned, relief should be given against an additional sales tax of 25 per cent. With effective economies practised, not 1-8 cents on the dollar economies, there would be no necessity for extra taxation, as was stated by the hon. member for Greenwood. He made that statement several days ago. Since not one minister of the crown has risen to challenge it, all one can conclude is that it is correct.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall delay the house but a few minutes. Since this budget is designed to accommodate a huge war preparation, it can hardly be expected to please one and all. I am sure that it meets with the general approval of the Canadian public. The opposition members are fully aware of the necessity for raising such huge sums. While criticizing the government severely, they have offered little advice as to how such sums could be raised or should be raised. Last evening when the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) rose in his place, I thought that perhaps he did have the solution. From the number of questions which he asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), I fear that the Social Credit party does not have the answer either.
I agree with some hon. members that perhaps there was room for an increase on the tax on liquor, which after all is a luxury and should be used only when the necessities of life have been provided. Last year the people in the province of Ontario spent in excess of $118 million in government liquor stores. I do not believe this sum includes the amount spent on cheaper beverages such as beer and wine. A tax increase in this area could possibly have had a twofold effect. It would have decreased the consumption, and made labour available for more essential industries.
The fact that the minister has decided to allow union dues to be deducted from the total earnings for income tax purposes gives me very great pleasure. I am sure that this removes from the statutes of Canada what has been said by many, and appears to me, to be class legislation.
It has been said that the tax on electrical appliances will weigh most heavily on newly married couples. I think we must not forget the fathers and mothers who have three and four children, who do not necessarily have all these facilities but certainly have all the

The Budget-Mr. Byrne budgetary difficulties of raising a large family.
I feel that none can escape this terrific burden of the defence preparation; it falls heavily on the nation as a whole.
I wish to develop what I consider to be one of the prime objectives of this battle against inflation. With ten per cent of our national production going in the direction of war expenditures, and without any appreciable increase in our total national production except in terms of dollar values, a reduction in our standard of living is almost inevitable. All the money in the world cannot buy the things that do not exist. If we were to distribute every earned dollar of profits, savings, and investments to the consuming public for the next year, we would not increase the goods available. The standard of living would continue to decline until we were able to find a means of increasing production. The exception, of course, would be the amount by which we were able to import from other countries by reason of the fantastic prices we would be prepared to offer. This may sound like poor reasoning, but I am simply trying to prove that unless we increase our national production by something in excess of ten per cent we cannot escape a reduction in our living standards. This alone will not stem the rising cost of living, but at least it will provide the materials for continued high living.
It has been said many times in this house that higher wages are the cause of inflation. I challenge this assertion, Mr. Speaker. The necessity for extremely high wage demands is but another symptom of the inflation or shortage of consumer goods. You show me an establishment where wages and conditions are poor, in relation to the whole, and I will show you an inefficient operation. High priced and a high quality labour encourages the development of better machines. Labour's continued desire for better conditions has always been, and will continue to be, a stimulus to industry to mechanize and modernize. The ability of the operators of industry to pay differs widely because of world and local market conditions. The unions must be left free to strike the best bargain possible for the employees concerned. I believe that many labour leaders, and the majority of the rank and file, seldom ask for or insist upon more than industry and the general public can afford to pay. In my opinion it is yet the only equitable way to distribute the wealth of the industries whose profits depend largely upon foreign markets.
The deferred depreciation plan provided in the budget will no doubt have the desired effect of deferring expenditures on gadgets, frills and a general dressing up of the

establishment. I am somewhat apprehensive of the long run effect it may have upon our standards. It will mean a further set-back in capital expenditures coming so quickly on the heels of a six-year delay consequent upon the last great war. This may have an adverse effect upon our living standards. Our rapidly increasing population, without an equal expansion of capital expenditures for increasing the productive capacity of consumer goods and farm machinery, will tend towards further shortages. This could increase the pressure on the inflationary spiral.
It has been said by leading economists, and many times in this house, that inflation is an enemy of force equal to any military power which we may face. That being so, any factors which may contribute to a lessening of production must not be overlooked, and conversely any factors which may tend to increase our productivity must be given consideration. While our valiant soldiers are fighting and dying on the battlefields, let us ask ourselves if we are doing everything in our power to win the battle against inflation on the economic field at home. It is not so much controls and a controlled economy that is needed most, but a measure of self-denial and the will to produce. How is this to be brought about? I would say first that we must make sure that the steel, which is presently in extremely short supply, is allotted in such a manner that it finds its way into the many labour saving devices and machines. We must adopt measures most likely to create amicable labour relations between employer and employee by an educational policy sponsored by our Department of Labour. I feel that this could go a long way towards the establishment of joint production committees such as were in existence during the last war, many of which- are still in operation today and doing excellent work. They could discuss production problems, review individual suggestions and make awards for useful applications for labour and material savings, as is being done in many of those committees in operations that continue that plan. They could encourage industry to adopt job simplification and method studies and could work toward the abandonment of old and obsolete rules which, in many ways, strangle progress.
I would suggest the exemption from income tax of all earnings acquired on an incentive and overtime basis and of all income earned in addition to regular yearly wages and salaries. At least if this were not possible, an alternative incentive would be to reduce the taxation on such income. That is to say anyone who is prepared to put additional

effort into productive capacity will not be put in a position of pyramiding his earnings for income tax purposes, something which has a repressive effect on individual initiative.
I would suggest calling a halt to the present practice of compulsory retirement of able-bodied employees at 60 and 65 and urge re-employment of those now retired who are willing and able to take positions in industry. Women who have no family ties should be encouraged to return to industry wherever possible. But we have those who are now on statutory fixed incomes and they must be looked after at the earliest possible moment if they are to continue to suffer under this present inflationary condition. I would urge that steps be taken immediately to carry out the recommendations of the old age security committee, that supplementary payments be made and that the means test be abolished at the earliest possible moment.
Leaving the general economic scene for a moment, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) who in an exceedingly able manner showed the precarious position that the western coal industry is in today. This situation is indeed serious; and before huge sums of public money are expended on such projects as the St. Lawrence waterway, I would suggest that we should make a complete and thorough survey of the economic conditions of both the far east and the far west. This is not to say that I am opposed in principle to the St. Lawrence seaway; but before accepting the scheme in toto, I should first wish to be assured that this heavy capital debt, running perhaps for generations, would not outweigh the benefits of the transportation facilities it would provide the nation. It is, of course, indisputable that water transportation is vastly more economical when the Creator and nature provide the channel; but it is Quite probable that this big ditch may forever put a burden on the Canadian public.
Is it necessary at this time that the iron ore of Labrador be brought to central Canada for the production of steel for the western provinces? Would it not be advisable first to investigate the possibility of a steel industry in the west where much of this material is consumed? The coal produced in western Canada, particularly in the Femie district, is particularly suitable for coking and blast furnace purposes. East Kootenay, of which Femie is a part, has all the natural resources necessary for such a development; and the markets in the prairie provinces and on the Pacific coast are constantly expanding. Farm machinery production has always been
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon a heavy user of steel, while gas and oil pipe lines will be needed in ever-increasing quantities.
There are some deposits of hematite ore in the Kootenays, and also an extremely large iron sulphide deposit, millions of tons of which have been milled and are lying in storage near the Sullivan mill at Kimberley in Kootenay East. Many more millions of tons can be produced and 500 tons daily are going into storage at that point. Generally, this iron sulphide is not considered to be a useful iron ore; but recent developments in that area, in the plans for building a fertilizer plant at Kimberley, changed the picture considerably, The roasting of iron sulphide for the production of sulphuric acid leaves a residue of iron oxide low in sulphur that can be utilized for blast furnaces. This sulphuric acid, by the way, is used in the production of fertilizer for the western provinces and export markets. Limestone, a raw material which is necessary in the operation of a blast furnace, is also available in the nearby Kootenay area.
I wish to commend this extremely important project to the attention of the house and to the government, and to ask that they give its possibilities serious consideration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget speech, delivered last Tuesday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), has been both a surprise and a disappointment. In fact, following the oft repeated declarations of friendship by members of the government for the labouring classes, nobody could expect that the proposed changes in the Income Tax Act would strike first and above all at the householder's budget. That is one reason for our surprise.
The unconcern, inaction and inconsistency of the authorities in the face of the present economic confusion are the causes of our disappointment.
Mr. Speaker, one of the first items of our defence program should be the fight against inflation. The government, however, is not giving that serious problem all the attention it deserves. No efficient steps have been taken to curb the excessive rise in the cost of living. What steps are suggested to prevent the situation from deteriorating even more? None, or very few. The authorities justify their inaction by repeating everywhere that other countries are faced with the same evil, that we are not the only ones who must grapple with this problem and that this thought should relieve our anxiety and put an end to our representations.

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon
The people, especially the workers, whose salaries have hardly increased since the war, are frantic. The necessities of life have reached a fantastic price, savings disappear, pensions, annuities and allowances, everything goes.
A worried public requests the government to take steps to stem this artificial wave of prosperity which absorbs savings and forces labour unions to ask for trade controls.
Unfortunately, price and wage controls alone cannot stop inflation. Such steps can bring temporary relief but, sooner or later, unless one strikes at the root causes of this capitalistic vice, powerful forces will break loose with such fury that no one will be able to curb them. A tied-down safety valve on the boiler won't hold the steam in check very long if you keep shovelling fuel into the fire box.
The government, whose duty it is to protect the public, should find means to remove the tremendous pressure of this increase.
Waiting to see what the effect will be of the United States government's orders in that respect, is to adopt the policy of the ostrich. A people who imitate others must necessarily lag behind.
Our ministers have no right to undertake, with the taxpayers' money, experiments as costly as these when immediate assistance is needed everywhere.
It is painful to note that, as far back as 1948, when the cost of living index stood at 155-0, the bureau of statistics, following an investigation bearing on the year ending August 31, proved that in Montreal 526,000 families and independent persons, with incomes in the neighbourhood of $3,000, were unable to make ends meet and that the average deficit was $8.19.
On the whole, since the publication of this report, the cost of living index has gone up 25 per cent. It is not hard to realize the plight of housewives and breadwinners at this time when the food index has gone up by 133-9.
In five years, the cost of meat has increased fourfold, while clothing, fuel and lighting also show a sharp increase.
A remarkable fact, however, is that while the salary cheque is too small to allow for proper family nourishment, dividends declared by various companies are higher than ever, and their profits greater than ever before in their history.
The Minister of Finance-
Writes UAction Catholique.
-does not seem to think that inflation has already been hard enough on the low-income taxpayers. He wants to pave the way for inflation, to help it along.

Viewed in that light, the sales tax increase is the worst thing that could happen to the Canadian people at this time, especially those who are unable to increase their income within a short time.
As a matter of fact, the 25 per cent increase in the sales tax, besides being inflationary, adds to the existing burden of taxation. It is an anti-social, vexatious and unfair tax, that should be abolished. Levied directly on the consumer, it adds to the cost of goods in strict ratio to its fixity, but when applied at the manufacturer's level it spirals up. In most instances, the dollar thereby extorted by the treasury costs the consumer three, four and even five dollars. For instance, the publicity, the advertising which enters for a certain proportion in the cost of any product, is taxed.
This tax on advertising means a further addition to the price the customer has to pay for the goods. At the various levels, wholesaler, distributor, jobber and retailer, the sales tax is applied several times, and this accounts for the frightful spread between the factory price and the retail price. The sales tax is a dreadful evil. I believe it should be replaced by increased import duties on wine and liquor.
Both in peacetime and in emergencies there is no respite for the Canadian taxpayer who last year contributed approximately $3,600 million in municipal, provincial and federal taxes. In 1952, the tax bill will exceed $4 billion. Of this tremendous taxation in a country of 14 million people, the federal government, true to the turn of mind of our centralists, takes the lion's share, or two-thirds. There remains 20 per cent for the ten provincial governments and 13 per cent for the 4,000 municipalities of this country.
Ten years ago, for example, the taxes collected at the three levels of government barely exceeded a billion dollars, one-half of which went to the federal government. 20 per cent to the provinces and 30 per cent to the municipalities. But the situation has changed considerably. The authorities do not seem to care if the municipalities, whose administration is the closest to the population and who are therefore in the best position to help our citizens, are incapable of balancing their budget and cannot meet their obligations, having been deprived of practically all their sources of revenue.
. Taxes which, normally, should fill their tills are diverted into the coffers of the federal government who uses them to further aims

infinitely more dangerous for the security of individuals and families than those pursued by municipal councils.
Those who claim that our cities, towns, and villages are not well run, since they have to report deficits year after year, forget that the property tax is practically their only source of revenue.
Far from correcting that abnormal situation, the government overtaxes our people, both directly and indirectly. The latter process, more cunning and hypocritical, is none the less quite distressing. Indirect taxation comprises chiefly excise duties on liquor, tobacco, cigarettes, automobiles, gasoline, furs, electrical appliances and countless items wrongly classed as luxuries, such as refrigerators, washing machines, radios, stoves, and so on. In many cases, customs duties add a substantial amount which has to be paid by the buyers.
The tax on home appliances is particularly hard on large families who rely on those articles to make housekeeping easier. Through this tax. an extremely heavy tribute is asked from the mother. It shows contempt for family life. The last budget is one of the worst, the most unfair people with modest means have had to bear for the past ten or fifteen years.
That was written in L'Action Catholique of April 12.
At a time when modern democracy should emphasize the part played by the family, the oldest organic cell in the world, and protect it because it is the best stabilizing factor, the family is overburdened with taxes.
The budget before us is directed against the family. The wealthy and the unmarried are treated with consideration but those classes of society the most in need of protection and support are burdened more heavily still.
According to a newspaper, a study by a group of economists shows that there are 150 taxes on the manufacture and sale of a lady's hat, 200 on a well-tailored dress, 120 on a man's suit and 150 on a loaf of bread.
On each package of cigarettes, the people of Chicoutimi will now pay 25 cents in taxes and over $1,000 on the purchase price of a $2,000 automobile.
For having failed to distinguish between the legal and technical aspects of our traditional economy, our politicians have passed from legitimate intervention to a deadly monopoly in the purely economic sphere. War placed all resources under government jurisdiction, it gave the state a governing hand in
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon our economy, it transformed certain activities into public utilities and afforded an opportunity of practising paternalism, that doctrine so dear to socialists.
The dominion government always finds an excuse to lay hands on other people's money.
Since the government invaded the field of income tax in 1917, it has collected from that source a total of nearly $11 billion, to which the excess profits tax adds some $3 billion. From June 1941 to 1950, it has collected $184 million in succession duties, $30 million of which were paid in 1950. Succession duties represent the real tax on capital. Yet, we ought to maintain legacies intact and prevent the state from absorbing, bit by bit, and from one generation to the next, the wealth of the country in such a way that it can no longer maintain itself.
The moral aspect of family capital is that it represents savings, that is, privations. It represents thousands of small pleasures and diversions of which parents have deprived themselves in order to leave their children in a better position. It is immoral to tax this effort as the dominion government has done and is still doing.
It must be remembered here that the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec alone paid 73 per cent of the total of $1,300,781,000 which personal and corporation income taxes and succession duties have brought to the federal treasury in 1950. The eight other provinces paid only $346,334,000 or less than the province of Quebec alone, which paid $354,000,000.
May I be permitted, in passing, to mention that in 1948, 12,300 persons or companies from Chicoutimi county, whom it is my privilege to represent in this house, paid the federal government $2,403,000 out of a total income of $32,064,000. I might add that Chicoutimi county included, in 1948, the county of Lapointe, represented today by my hon. friend opposite. We are in fourth place among the income tax payers of the province of Quebec, after Montreal, Quebec and St. Maurice. We are therefore entitled to mention it and to voice our grievances. Why are we taxed? For war. It has become a habit with the government.
Since 1935 the Liberal party has spent billions of dollars for military purposes. War has become its specialty. The tragedy begins once more. Nothing is changed. The same actors are once again found in the principal parts. The very same generation of men and

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon women is once more being called upon to pay-in blood and money the cost of our overseas ventures. Canada has taken its place among war-mongering nations and our ministers, unable to restore peace to the world, have decided that we would participate in the Korean conflict while awaiting another theatre of operations.
The Minister of Finance is taxing us to send our young people to their death in Asia. He is taxing us to produce planes and bombs in order that our Atlantic pact commitments may be carried out. What if the old age pension is not increased, what if invalids receive no financial assistance from the state, what if urgent works are abandoned, what if people are weary of hearing talk of massacres, rations and taxes? Those are things of no concern! We will make war alongside the United States if, when and wherever they will it, against Russia or China or anybody else.
We have lived through a period when our leaders were all but ready to canonize Stalin. Today the idea is to take him down from the pedestal where our prayers had put him.
Our leaders are wise, they have much experience. Their propaganda is clever. We fought for the freedom of nations during the second world war with our friends in Moscow. We shall fight again for freedom, but against them this time and with our friends in South Korea or elsewhere. It is always in the name of liberty that people are led to slavery. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) chooses our enemies, and the Canadian people foot the bill for these changes. Our international policy is decided by dreamers who want Canada to put forth a war effort beyond her capacity and the Minister of Finance has to find the billions necessary to satisfy their unrestrained ambitions.
If those who are responsible for international policy worked as hard to ensure peace as they do to launch us on a new crusade, if the representatives who attend the meetings of the United Nations council gave more importance to moral values and to the true destiny of the world, if God held the place which belongs to Him in people's hearts and minds and at the meetings of the poor human beings who are vainly seeking a solution to the world's problems, there would be on this earth more happiness and welfare, less hardship and less tears. This armament race will be very costly.	,


The crown has squandered the goods it had acquired with the money of the people from 1939 to 1945. Plants, ships, equipment, material which had cost hundreds of millions to the workers of the country have been sold for a few thousand dollars. Political favourites or privileged companies have been given, so to speak, water power installations, telephone and telegraph lines, equipment, etc. And now we must start all over again, building airfields, machine shops and other plants, once more with the people's money.
Once more, billions of dollars will be thrown to the four winds for the benefit of munition makers and] international monopolistic profiteers.
I refuse to subscribe to such aims and to believe that it is on the battlefields of the Orient that we shall clinch the defeat of communism. We want peace, a noble, serene and dignified peace which will free our people of the crushing burden of taxes and allow them to progress in peace and honour. We wish to work, to suffer and to pay taxes to assure life but not death. I will therefore vote in favour of the amendment.
