subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take advantage of the opportunity afforded by this debate on the budget to give hon. members of this house a brief description of my riding and to inform them of our problems and our needs, a duty which perhaps I have delayed too long.
The riding of Burin-Burgeo extends along the south coast of Newfoundland, from Cape Ray in the southwest corner to Come-By-Chance in Placentia bay and includes all the numerous islands for which this beautiful bay is noted.
History records that as far back as 1621 Placentia bay was the base of operations for the famous pirate, Captain Peter Easton, and on the picturesque island of Oderin, where he was reported to have his headquarters, a mysterious oaken floor still exists at the bottom of a small salt water pond and is considered to be one of the several engineering feats attributed to this famous sailor.
Legend has it that one of Captain Easton's ships was sunk in a battle with another famous pirate by the familiar name Cruick-shank and that this shipload of treasure still rests on the ocean bottom beneath the cliffs of Cape Roger head, six miles across the bay from Oderin.

Pirate gold is also supposed to be buried in beautiful Cape Roger harbour, but all attempts to unearth it have been frustrated by mysterious water spouts. These spouts rush up through the sandy loam when the hole reaches a depth of seven or eight feet and continue to rise to a height of ten feet above sea level.
I mention these stories to emphasize the fact that Newfoundland is an old province with a history dating back centuries before that of the mainland and her communities are steeped in history and very rich in folklore.
Incidentally, I am hoping that these names may catch the attention of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) because I have been trying for some time to have a guardian placed on Cape Roger river and if the salmon are not sufficiently important, perhaps the buried treasure might provide an added inducement.
The riding which I have the honour to represent is a veritable paradise for both the sportsman and the artist. All along the one thousand miles of coast line the scenery is magnificent. High rocky cliffs rise perpendicular to the sea in their stark naked and rugged, beauty. Between these steep cliffs, so narrow as to be almost imperceptible, are numerous openings which run inland for miles, rivalling the fjords of Norway and ending in pools where beautiful salmon rivers cascade into the sea. In season these rivers and pools are teaming with salmon and salt water trout. A mile or so in the interior the country abounds with moose, caribou, partridge, rabbits and other game. The provincial government is already working to develop these natural attractions but it will take some time before they will be able to cater satisfactorily to the tourist business. Many fine salmon rivers are without protection of any kind, and it is hoped that before too long guardians will be placed not only on Cape Rogers river but on many others.
To get a picture of my riding you must visualize approximately one thousand miles of coast line studded with some 260 settlements perched close to the sea, their peaceful harbours dotted with tiny fishing boats riding at their moorings. Along the shore line nestling close to the sea the simple fishers' cottages though often poor and humble nevertheless extend unfailing welcome and boundless hospitality. In these 260 settlements live some 44,000 of the best people in the world, fisher folk who are the very salt of the earth.
50709-143J
The Budget-Mr. Carter They live close to nature and close to their God. They ask so little from life in this age of materialism that their humility is both touching and inspiring. They ask nothing but the bare necessities of life, and I know from personal experience that for years many of them have had to be content with much less than that. It is a great honour and privilege to serve such people, and I pray that my efforts will be worthy of their trust.
When the great issue of confederation came up my constituents gave it wholehearted support. They remembered the time when they had to exist on a government dole of 7 cents a day. They remembered the relative prosperity of their brothers fishing out of Lunenburg, of their relatives settled in Halifax, Toronto and Vancouver. They remembered the nice things in Eaton's and Simpson's catalogues on which no duty would have to be paid. They remembered the coastal services which they had enjoyed fifteen and twenty years ago, and which they had to forfeit along with their responsible government. They looked at their dilapidated wharves and breakwaters upon which not a cent had been spent for fifteen or twenty years, and they thought of the public services, the navigational aids and communication system enjoyed by the maritime provinces.
Then they reasoned: Surely confederation will bring us back at least the kind of services we used to enjoy twenty and thirty years ago, and perhaps a little better. They pictured Canada as a young giant just beginning to realize his strength and eager to use it by extending a helping hand to a weaker and less fortunate brother. I mention all these things to dispel any notion that Newfoundlanders voted for confederation to get family allowances. That was something outside their experience, and many actually doubted their existence.
Two years have now passed, and what is the position today? I think that ninety per cent of the people are still satisfied that confederation was the wisest and best course. They know now that the family allowance is a reality, and they have had time to realize what a blessing it really is. Our children are now comfortably and respectably clad irrespective of family income, and school attendance has become stabilized at a much higher level, so that the benefits of family allowances alone as an investment in the youth of our province are sufficient to justify the wisdom of confederation.
The social benefits of unemployment insurance, old age pensions and pensions for the blind are other blessings that are very greatly
2234	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Carter appreciated by our people, and we hope that in time it will be possible to extend unemployment insurance to include our fishermen. Then there -are the federal health benefits which I understand totalled $1 million last year. In my riding alone this has helped to provide three clinical boats whereby doctors can make periodical tours of their districts, and patients requiring hospitalization can be transported to the nearest cottage hospital to receive treatment under a provincial system of subsidized medicine. A new cottage hospital is being built at Channel with federal assistance at the rate of $1,000 per bed.
Then there are the improvements to our harbour facilities, marine installations, public wharves, breakwaters, slipways and protection works. In the majority of settlements this is the first money to be spent on public works for over fifteen years. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is not used to being applauded for his efforts, but I feel that my constituents would want me to voice their appreciation to his department for the sympathetic consideration which has been given to these needs, and the improvements that are being accomplished through the untiring efforts of their district engineer and a small but efficient staff. They have not been able to accede to all our requests but it is very evident that they are carrying out a well considered plan to distribute their efforts over the whole province of Newfoundland as evenly and fairly as their limited staff and circumstances will permit. In this connection I should like to urge the Minister of Public Works to increase the staff of the Newfoundland office in order to alleviate the unfair burden which now falls upon the district engineer, and thus expedite the work of his department.
In looking back on confederation I believe that at least ninety per cent of our people, and possibly more, would appraise the benefits of confederation as I have outlined them and would feel that it was the right thing to do. That is not to say, however, that there have not been disappointments, and bitter disappointments too. The greatest disappointment of all was that the substantial reduction in our cost of living, to which all had looked forward with such great expectations, failed to materialize. This was due to a rise in prices on the mainland which Coincided with the date of union, together with the fact that Canadian National Railways chose to take advantage of loose wording in the terms of union to apply a system of freight rates far in excess of the preferential maritime rates which everyone, including those who negotiated and signed the terms of union, understood would apply to New-
[Mr. Carter.)

foundland. Recently the board of transport commissioners decided this question in favour of Newfoundland, but in the meantime Newfoundlanders had paid several million dollars more than they would otherwise have paid on goods brought into the province. Mail and passenger service have improved considerably, but in spite of the improvement they are not a great deal better than the service Newfoundlanders enjoyed twenty or thirty years ago, before they were forced to give up responsible government.
Several new post offices have been opened in my riding and a fairly satisfactory service has been extended to other settlements by including them in rural water routes, a kind of travelling post office. We are grateful to the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) and his efficient staff for these improvements, and for the courteous and sympathetic consideration his officials give to all our requests. However, many difficulties and even hardships arise from the fact that regulations governing postal operations on the mainland are not at all applicable to Newfoundland. A good example of this is a regulation requiring a distance of two miles between post offices. This may be all right on the mainland where settlements are connected by road, but in Newfoundland very few settlements are connected by road. In order to get to a post office one must launch a boat and row over two miles of salt water. That is quite a different matter. When the men are away fishing the women and children have to do this. In view of the hardships and dangers involved, especially in stormy weather, I feel that this regulation should be relaxed or eliminated altogether as far as Newfoundland is concerned.
Then there is the system of remuneration, which is based upon the sale of stamps. On the mainland there is probably a direct relationship between the value of the stamps sold and the amount of work the postmaster has to do. In Newfoundland there is no such relationship, because the incoming mail is usually ten to fifteen times greater than the outgoing. Family allowances have made ready cash available to parents, and a large proportion of that cash finds its way to the mail order houses. As a result the number of incoming parcels has multiplied many times. This state of affairs is likely to continue indefinitely. This increased mail order business has resulted in increased c.o.d. deliveries, insured parcels, money orders and so on, all of which have no relation at all to the stamps sold. In addition, some postmasters have to sort and distribute mail for other smaller offices which sell their own stamps. As a consequence of all these factors which do not obtain to the same degree on

the mainland, the system of remuneration based upon stamp revenue is very unfair to Newfoundland postmasters. The same is true of rental rates of post office accommodation. Probably the maximum rates are satisfactory; but when you consider that in Newfoundland soft coal costs $25 per ton, the minimum rate of $1 per month is very low when heat, light and cleaning have to be provided as well.
While I am on this subject I should like to bring to the attention of this house the plight in which our 437 postmaster-telegraphers find themselves as a result of confederation. Prior to confederation they were civil servants and as such enjoyed certain privileges such as sick leave with pay and vacations with relief operators supplied at government expense. Today as a result of confederation, though their pension rights are safeguarded by the terms of union, they have lost their civil service status and their sick leave and vacation privileges, which had considerable value in terms of dollars and cents. As a result most postmaster-telegraphers are not able to take an annual vacation for the simple reason that they cannot afford to pay travelling, board and salary expenses for a relief operator, and in consequence their health is beginning to suffer. More serious still is the plight of those who need medical treatment, surgical operations and hospitalization, and must do without because they cannot afford the cost of a relief operator.
The sad thing about this whole affair is that now no one has any responsibility for them. The Canadian National Telegraphs regard them as postmasters. They are not telegraph employees, because the telegraph company merely rents their services from the Post Office Department. On the other hand the stamp revenue is too small to qualify them as full-time postmasters, so they are only part-time postmasters and part-time telegraphers, through between the two they are full-time employees and have more than a full-time job.
There is also the erroneous idea that the salaries of these people have increased considerably since confederation. Even if this were true it would be only fair and right because the work they have to do has multiplied many times, but from my own investigation I know it is not true. About one-third are actually better off. Another third have received increases just about sufficient to offset the loss of free vacations and sick leave with pay. The remainder get exactly the same salary as before, but the loss of sick leave and vacations with pay makes them definitely worse off than before confederation. Furthermore, their telegraph
The Budget-Mr. Carter
duties require them to work overtime and on Sundays, for which they are unable to claim any extra remuneration. I hope the ministers concerned will do everything possible to find a remedy for this situation because this state of affairs, while it may conform to a strict, literal interpretation of the terms of union, is definitely not in accord with the spirit of union nor with the spirit embodied in the terms of union.
Another big disappointment is the lack of Canadian National Telegraph service to smaller settlements. Most of these communities expected that confederation would restore those telegraphic and telephonic communications which they enjoyed some twenty years or more ago but which they lost along with their responsible government. These hopes have not been realized, and worse still there seems to be little chance that they will ever be realized, because Canadian National Telegraphs is organized to operate on a profit basis and most of these small offices would operate at a loss.
On the other hand there is a definite need for these telegraph and telephone services, a need all the more urgent because of lack of roads and other means of communication. We all know that a good system of telecommunications is absolutely essential to progress. In my province it is also essential to offset the handicap of isolation, to send a call for medical aid in time of sickness or accidents, to enable the bank fisherman to contact his family when his ship puts into port. How can we measure human values in terms of dollars and cents? Of what significance is a monetary deficit when human lives are at stake? During the last war these little offices were the means of saving the lives of many of our airmen who had to make forced landings in out of the way places. They were also the means of forwarding much valuable information to defence headquarters concerning submarines and other suspicious craft. In fact, the excellent work done by the aircraft detection corps would have been utterly impossible without the aid of these small stations. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these small telegraph and telephone stations constitute an essential part of our defence program. This fact alone is sufficient to justify an expansion of the system. The importance of these small telegraph offices cannot be judged in terms of their revenue, because without them the revenues of the larger offices would be much less. It was gratifying to me to learn in a recent committee on railways and shipping that the Canadian National Telegraph Company has now initiated a definite policy with regard to the expansion of these services.

The Budget-Mr. Carter
The coastal services of the Canadian National Railways have increased their frequency to a little better than that enjoyed twenty years ago, but the number of ports served still totals only 73 out of 260. The ship used on the Placentia bay service has accommodation for only eight passengers, while the number requiring transportation averages around 30. I travelled on this ship and saw the terrible conditions that obtain. Passengers are forced to sit up all night huddled together in narrow alleyways or crouching on their suitcases. How could anyone with red blood in his veins help but feel a sense of indignation at seeing his fellow men subjected to such treatment? Conditions during stormy weather and the winter season are beyond description. They are made bearable only by the skill of the captain and his crew, and their general solicitude for their fellow man which often compels them to give up their berths to passengers thus sacrificing their own much needed rest and comfort.
I am satisfied that the local management is in no way to blame for this state of affairs. The blame rests with the mainland offices where policy in these matters is decided by people who, I believe, are fully aware of this situation. I realize that it must be a terrible dilemma to the Canadian National Railways to be required to operate as a private enterprise on one hand and as a public utility on the other, but nevertheless, for humanitarian reasons, these conditions which I have described from personal experience should not be permitted to exist.
The urgent need of at least three small passenger and cargo boats is apparent when it is realized that the Canadian National Railways in Newfoundland not only do not have sufficient passenger boats to take care of present traffic, but they have no spare boat in reserve in case of accident or emergency. Should one of the present ships be lost, the whole coastal service would collapse. To make matters worse, one of the ships now in service is over fifty years old and is due to be retired; another is approaching retirement age. We are all very pleased that a new ferry is being provided for the gulf service, but there is serious doubt of the wisdom of building at this time such a large ship as contemplated, requiring such extensive terminal facilities, harbour installations and improvements. Experienced captains and navigators have expressed serious doubts as to whether such a large ship can be safely manoeuvred during bad weather in the small space available in the terminal port.
On my way to attend this session I was met by a delegation from Channel and Port TMr. Carter.]
aux Basques, who felt that the proposed change in the location of terminals would have an adverse effect on the life of these twin towns. They expressed surprise and indignation that Canadian National Railways should finalize plans for such extensive changes without even consulting the town council or some local organization. I believe it would be wiser to build a smaller ferry, which in conjunction with the ships now in service would be big enough to take care of the peak load traffic but still small enough to use present installations. The money saved would provide for the coastal service those smaller ships which are needed just as urgently as the new ferry. Later on a second ferry might be provided if the need arose. The ships that the new ferry is supposed to release are not suitable for the coastal service because they are too big for most of the harbours and cannot be operated economically in that type of service.
In view of the important part played by the merchant navy in the two world wars, the provision of these small ships could be regarded as almost an essential part of our defence preparation. Because the need is so urgent, I plead with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to give serious consideration to these proposals.
Related to this subject is the case of wharfingers, of whom there are a considerable number. Prior to confederation the Newfoundland government paid these people for the handling of government-owned packages for the federal government without ingers have been required to handle parckages for the federal government without any remuneration whatever. It does not seem right morally, and it is certainly not democracy, that any person should be required to work for nothing or to give his services for nothing, even to the national government. I understand that statutory authority is lacking whereby the government is able to make such payments, but surely that is a simple matter to remedy. I trust that this little problem will be solved on the basis of what is right, rather than what is legal.
We are grateful, too, for what the Department of Transport has done to improve our navigational aids. But many more fog alarms, gas and whistle buoys and radio beacons are needed to afford our fishermen a standard of protection comparable to that enjoyed by the maritime provinces.
A few weeks ago my good friend the member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) described to this house the terrible plight of our inshore fishermen owing to the market price of salt cod dropping from an average of $14 per quintal in 1949 to an average of $7 per quintal in I960. Some

received even less than that. The cost of living is still on the increase, and we hope that steps will be taken to ensure that our inshore fishermen receive a fair -return for their catch. In Ottawa fresh cod retails for 39 cents per pound, yet the fisherman receives only 3 or 4 cents per pound. Salt cod retails at 49 cents per pound, and the fisherman gets 10 to 12 cents per pound. I should explain, Mr. Speaker, that this fish is from the maritimes and not from Newfoundland. I understand that mainland firms are reluctant to buy Newfoundland fish from the marketing organization known as NAFEL. It is difficult to believe that processing and transportation can account for such tremendous price spreads. I feel that this is a situation which might well be investigated under the combines act.
In his reference to merchants, I am sure that the member for St. John's West did not intend to imply that all merchants exploit the fishermen. Possibly some do, but there are many who do not. Many merchants have invested their profits in the fishery and sustained heavy losses in the interests of the fishermen. There are also many smaller shopkeepers who take staggering risks in supplying for the fishery, and they get only a small commission for collecting the fish for the exporters.
Recently the restriction on the shooting of turrs was debated in this house. This is also another matter of great concern to our people for which we hope a satisfactory solution can be obtained.
I mention all these matters, Mr. Speaker, not in any spirit of complaining, but because they are a source of real dissatisfaction to a large number of my constituents and I feel I would be failing in my duty if I did not direct attention to them. Trivial though they may appear to be, nevertheless they are very important because they concern people and they represent points where our people feel that democracy has ceased to identify itself with their needs.
When Lincoln defined democracy as government of the people, by the people and for the people, he left no doubt that concern for people constitutes the very essence of democracy. Like the Sabbath, democracy was made for man and not man for democracy. I think we sometimes tend to forget this great truth. When we set up a democratic machine and try to fit man into it, when- we subordinate man to profits, to political considerations, to expediency or to any other thing, how much better are we than the Kremlin which sets up [DOT] the state above the individual?
The Budget-Mr. Carter
We may have all the exterior trappings of democracy; we may go through the democratic motions as often as we like; but unless we are motivated by a genuine care for the needs of mankind, in our own land and everywhere else, we do not have true democracy and we fool nobody, except perhaps ourselves.
I hope that the government will be able to give favourable consideration to the matters which I have brought to their attention and which mean so much to my people. We realize that our coastal and telegraph services cannot be brought up to standard overnight; but those conditions-such as those with regard to the postmaster-telegraphers, the wharfingers, the Placentia bay coastal boat service, and the postal regulations-which are causing such unnecessary hardship should be remedied at once. Immediate action is necessary to convince our people that government is not indifferent to their needs and to restore their faith in democracy.
I should like to repeat that we are grateful for what has been done so far and we appreciate the benefits of confederation, particularly the social benefits; because we are like our brothers from Quebec in that our Newfoundland families are extremely close knit.
Here, Mr. Speaker, as an English-speaking Canadian I should like to say to my Frenchspeaking colleagues how grateful I am for them and for the people they represent. Their way of life and the emphasis which they have always placed on those deep spiritual values symbolized by the home, the church, family ties and simplicity of life, give them much in common with the people of my own province. I should like to say that we Newfoundlanders are proud to join with them and with the other provinces in working out, under God, the true destiny of our young and vigorous nation.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the true destiny of our nation is to give to the world a demonstration of true democracy-an inspired democracy that will capture the hearts and minds of the millions in Asia, in India, in Africa, and in Europe who are now searching for a form of government that will meet all their needs and aspirations. These millions leave no room for doubt that they are not at all impressed by the brand of democracy that we have demonstrated to them to date.
This new democracy, this true democracy, will put people before things and service before profits. Industry and business, management and labour, will be inspired by a motive higher than profits; and out of their

The Budget-Mr. Carter sense of responsibility for the nation and their caring for the needs of people will come that creative thinking which will solve our housing problems and stabilize the purchasing power of our dollar. The labourer will give an honest day's work in return for an honest day's pay, and the individual production of real wealth will increase. Instead of shortages there will be abundance for all our own needs and plenty left over to give to those who have not. Along with our gifts we will give our hearts so that our assistance may have a spiritual value as well as a material value.
Freedom of enterprise will not be the freedom of the jungle. There will be no strikes because all disputes will be settled on a basis of what is right instead of who is right. There will be no poverty because when everyone cares enough and shares enough, everyone will have enough. Honest prices and honest profits along with increased production per man will lower the cost of living. Communism will wither in the face of this superior idea by which it will be outmoded and outlived. Self control in the individual, which in its highest form is God control, will make government controls unnecessary; because the more that people govern themselves, the less they have to be governed.
Government will present issues to the people on a moral basis instead of on an economic, legal or political basis and people will be taken into partnership with government and fully briefed for the part they have to play. Individuals and organized groups will not bargain with their votes nor try to impose their will on the nation, nor will they seek advantages at the expense of others.
In parliament there will be total honesty between parties and between members: total honesty in debate, honesty of motives and honest admission of mistakes and failures. We can best preserve peace by removing the causes of war, and most of the causes of war, Mr. Speaker, lie within ourselves. This new order cannot be built without sacrifice. Temporarily we may have to sacrifice our standard of living. We shall certainly have to sacrifice our greed, our selfishness, our ambition and our comparative moral standards. We cannot build a new world and retain the old evils. We shall all have to change; because as I am, so is my nation. We shall have to learn to live on a basis of absolute moral standards. We shall have to match our external defence program by developing our internal defences of moral and spiritual strength; and we can do that only by exercising moral judgment and by making moral decisions.
This, Mr. Speaker, is my idea of true democracy. This is my blueprint for a new Canada. This I believe is Canada's true destiny. These are the things I want to fight for in my home, in my riding, in my province and in this parliament.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In my first words, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member from the tenth province on his wonderful address with reference to his constituency and the province of Newfoundland. I must say that I enjoyed it greatly indeed; but I want to give him this warning. If he expects this government to fulfil the terms of confederation, he will have to be on tap each session and demand the fulfilment of each one of those terms. This I know from past experience with reference to the province of Prince Edward Island.
Canada is taking part in the present momentous struggle with communism. Military preparedness must play a large part in the administration of this government. Hence the huge budget presented to this house on Tuesday, April 10, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It is equally important that our domestic problems are not entirely neglected; for instance, unemployment, old age pensioners, retired pensioners, the incapacitated and the helpless. Many of these are on starvation allowances at the present time. Without any interference with military preparedness, but by real co-operation, we could become producers by using our manpower who are not physically fit for military purposes or military training, and we could thus continue -and I address this remark to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier)-public works and other essentials both for war and for peace.
A question arises, and it is heard quite often: Is Canada at war? The answer to that question by some people is yes, and by other people it is no. We have had no declaration of war since 1939 when Canada declared war. But on the other hand, we have never had a declaration of peace; therefore we must still be at war. At any rate, our soldiers and airmen are fighting today; our men are in training; our sailors and our marines are all in the fray, and we are having casualties announced among our men, and some of them have made the supreme sacrifice. I repeat we must still be at war. Still our government is making great preparations, and I hope they are making preparations for a global war, which I also hope may never come.
I am glad to note that in this budget debate Mr. Speaker has allowed a very wide latitude of discussion. This enables one to speak with reference to his own province

and his own constituency. The budget is remarkable in a great many ways. Some of the statements that we have seen in the press since the budget was brought down have called it by a great many varied names. One of them was that it is a most senseless budget. When one looks at it he considers that there are many things in it, and also many surprises. When the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) was speaking the other night I noticed he said that one of the surprises to him was the discriminatory taxation on the fur industry. Another great surprise to me was that I did not find, either in the estimates or in the speech of the minister, any amount included for damages to Prince Edward Island because of the railway strike.
The legislative assembly of Prince Edward Island in an emergency session called on September 7, 1950, asked that the dominion government be assessed owing to the failure of the government to keep the Borden-Tormen-tine ferry in operation during the railway strike. It was a surprise to me that no reference was made to it in the budget, and I am inclined to believe that the Minister of Finance did not know that there was an election in sight in the province of Prince Edward Island, or a reference to it would have been made in the budget, or in the estimates.
Budgets come and budgets go. Since two of them have gone by I must say that there is some record in connection with this one. The minister has the record of producing three budgets in a year and thirteen days. I think this is a record that no other minister of finance of Canada has ever held. The first two are gone with the wind, and this one is remarkable in several ways. The budget is being criticized; yet it is claimed by the government side that it is a budget for economy. Perhaps it is, but I do not wish them to economize to the detriment of commitments they have made, which should be fulfilled.
I suppose the Minister of Public Works will now blame the Minister of Finance because public works such as the dominion building in Charlottetown, which has been promised for four years and more-in fact at the last two elections-

I suppose that must be treated as a hope. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that with all the power vested, as it is, in the ministers of the crown, when they start making arrangements for preparedness for war, I hope that they make a list of the provinces that have had nothing to do with the preparation for war, the supplying of materials for war-I am now speaking of the last war-and give them an opportunity to do some of that work at this time. For instance, I am hoping that Prince Edward Island will have an opportunity. During the last war, out of the hundreds of millions of dollars spent for war purposes, Prince Edward Island received something less than one-tenth of one per cent of the disbursements made to the upper provinces.
For years we have been struggling to get some further fulfilment of the terms of union. Now that provision is being made to spend vast sums of money, as set out in the estimates, for the erection of new plants, and the taking over of plants already in existence, this might be an opportune time for the government to implement the recommendations of the Andrew Rae Duncan commission of 1926. I have mentioned this matter before in connection with harbour improvements at Charlottetown, and the important recommendation respecting the marine railway slip at that city.
This marine railway slip should have been built long ago. It has been promised to us by all governments. Now would be the opportune time to have it built, because it would give our machine shops and foundries an opportunity in these days of preparation for war to do certain work on boats they have thus far been unable to do because of the lack of the marine railway slip. With the marine railway slip we could take care of the repairs connected with the Borden-Tormentine ferry service, and repairs to the

The Budget-Mr. McLure boats on the Wood Island-Caribou route. In addition to that there are in service boats such as the Brant, the Saurel and others, that are laid up during the winter, or are performing other tasks in the maritime provinces. In servicing these boats, in addition to smaller craft such as tugs, we would have a source of employment for, according to the estimate, some two hundred men annually. I say that now would be the time to make that expenditure so as to provide a service absolutely essential to Charlottetown. We need it so as to give employment to the men in the machine shops.
At the time of the last war we did obtain a few small subcontracts for the repairing of corvettes. Our men did an excellent job in all the work they had to do. However there was some work below the waterline they were not permitted to do. If some of the government contracts are to be decentralized, if some of the centralization which has worked to the detriment of the maritime provinces is to be eliminated, we would ask at this time consideration in respect to the building of this marine railway slip.
During the last war we did make repairs to some marine boats, and I am glad to say departmental records show that the workmanship was satisfactory, and that the cost of repairs done in the machine shops and foundries at Charlottetown was less than at any other point where similar repairs were done. This point in itself should be of interest to the government, and afford us an opportunity to have these public works built in Prince Edward Island, and more particularly in the city of Charlottetown.
I should like to say a few words on another matter. During the last war money was spent recklessly indeed. It was spent as Monte Carlo gamblers would have spent it, and without any incentive, apparently, to look after more than a few of the provinces of Canada while, at the same time, making it more difficult for the rest of us. However in Prince Edward Island when soldiers, sailors, fliers, food, bond purchasers and more taxes were required the people of that province did more per capita than those of any other province in Canada. That is a record of which we are proud, notwithstanding the fact that we were not given any work so that we might keep the labouring element of our population at home. They had to follow the contracts to cities in other provinces.

the second reading of Bill No. 177, to incorporate the Mercantile and General Reinsurance Company of Canada Limited.
Could we have an explanation of this bill?

This bill seeks to give incorporation to a company now carrying on business in England, which is known by a similar name. This company seeks to carry on its legitimate business of insurance and reinsurance in Canada, as they have been doing for some years in England. They merely seek subsidiary powers to carry on the reinsurance business in Canada. The types of insurance it is sought to carry on are fire insurance, accident insurance, aircraft insurance, automobile insurance, guarantee insurance and the usual types of business falling within the scope of that type of company. The bill

is drawn in accordance with the requirements of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, and carries the approval of the superintendent of insurance. The bill provides that substantial amounts will be deposited with the superintendent of insurance before the company commences to do business in this country.
I would therefore suggest that the bill be accorded second reading and referred to the committee on miscellaneous private bills.

I should like to make a few remarks on this bill and to ask the hon. member who introduced it if he will be kind enough when closing the debate on second reading to reply to some questions of a general nature which I should like to place before him.
Personally I welcome this bill, which on its face seems to simply seek to incorporate in Canada a company presently incorporated in the United Kingdom and which no doubt is already doing business in this country. I think that is a desirable thing to have done with these companies which at the moment are unincorporated branches of companies in other countries. I believe they should be incorporated in this country, because then shares will have to be offered to the public in Canada, and there will be Canadian directors and so on. This suggests two things. The first is the confidence of these companies in the future of Canada. The second is an increasing degree of control by Canadians over the affairs of corporations doing business in this country. These are both healthy trends, in my opinion.
The questions I should like to address to the hon. member who introduced the bill are these. First, what is the dollar volume of the annual business presently being done by the company in Canada, on the basis of which I presume it seeks incorporation? I do not imagine that if the company were doing only a small or relatively negligible amount of business in this country it would consider it worth while to incorporate. I should imagine the company hopes and intends to increase the volume of its business in Canada. If that is the object I think it is a desirable one. It is the object which on the face of it I attached to the desire to incorporate, and I should like confirmation of that fact and information as to the present volume of business being done.
Then I notice that all the persons seeking incorporation are residents of the city of Toronto. I should like to know whether any of these persons are at present directors of the company in England, or whether any person in Canada has been appointed a

director of the British company. Then, coming as I do from western Canada, where we have a great interest in industrial and commercial enterprise and expansion of all sorts I should like to know whether at present the company does any substantial amount of business in western Canada and whether, in view of the increased interest the company is showing in this country, it intends to make an effort to extend its business in the west. I suppose I have certain misgivings consequent upon the fact that according to section 1 of the bill all these gentlemen are from Toronto, and I wonder if they have that intimate knowledge of and unbounded confidence in the growth of western Canada in general and British Columbia in particular which is felt by those of us who know that country well.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the questions the hon. member is addressing to the sponsor of this bill would not more appropriately be asked in the committee to which the bill would be referred later.

Speaking to the point of order, apparently there are a few members of this committee who are not as interested in protecting the interests of western Canada as others are. This is the only opportunity the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) will have to obtain this information. Many of us from western Canada are vitally interested in these matters. I was particularly interested, for instance, in the question of the volume of business being done in western Canada, and I was also interested in whether or not any Canadians are directors of the British company.
I quite appreciate that it is not proper to have questions and answers at this stage, but I would point out that here we are being asked for approval of the principle on second reading.
And you approved that in your opening sentence.

That involves the adoption of a motion by this house. My approval would be based upon certain conclusions I have drawn from the nature of the bill itself, because we have not had a very extensive explanation by the hon. member who introduced it. Therefore before I give my formal approval' to second reading I should like the answers to those questions, to confirm or otherwise the conclusions I have drawn. That is why I am putting these questions. I do not intend to take up much time or to talk out the bill, even if that were possible. I just want to place certain questions and general conclusions before the hon. member

which I would like him to either confirm or deny, following which I will be able to make up my mind as to whether or not I, as one member of this house, should approve the bill on second reading.

On the point of order, I might say there is some substance in the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson). However, I think I should allow the questions to stand. The hon. member who is introducing the bill may not have the information, and it might be more appropriate to get the information in committee. If the hon. member can answer the questions, I think he should be given an opportunity of doing so. At this time I might say that I do not think the questions should be repeated by other hon. members, but the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has asked the questions and I will allow them to stand.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. There is one other matter on which I should like to make some remarks. In introducing the bill the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Cavers) referred to the carrying on of a general insurance business. That raises in my mind a question which is perhaps not very material, but on which he might enlighten me. I notice the name under which the company seeks incorporation is the Mercantile and General Reinsurance Company of Canada Limited. Of course, there is a fairly substantial difference between a straight insurance business, where a company accepting a direct risk charges for that risk a premium which is higher or lower in proportion as the risk is greater or less. There is quite a difference between that and the business of reinsurance where some companies who have issued policies of insurance accepting risk turn around to other groups and ask them if they will reinsure the company against a loss under the policy issued. It is quite a different type of business, and quite a different type of risk, in so far as reinsurance is concerned. The name of the company would give the impression it is going to undertake only the business of reinsurance. I would ask the hon. member who introduced the bill and made the statement, which seemed to me to imply the company was going to carry on the business of general insurance, whether there is a limitation. Does the company intend to undertake all forms of insurance, both direct and reinsurance, or will it confine its activities to one form or the other? If the hon. member can give the answers to those questions, Mr. Speaker, I for one would find them helpful indeed in making up my mind as to how to vote on the motion for second reading.

Mr. Speaker, any insurance company will carry on a business of reinsurance. Quite often a primary writer is asked to reinsure a risk, and he will take part of that risk. To handicap this insurance company applying for a reinsurance charter by asking the representatives to state whether they are ever going into the primary writing of insurance seems hardly fair. I do not think any group organizing a company would like to pin themselves down by saying they did not intend in the future to write primary risks. They are asking for a charter now to start as a reinsurance company. As a matter of fact, practically every primary writing insurance company does a reinsurance business today.

On a question of privilege; I am sure the hon. member would not want to take from my words an inference which was not there or which I did not intend. I did not intend to suggest that this company should be restricted to one or the other type-of business. I merely asked for information as to whether they desired to restrict themselves to one or the other type of business. I was not able to gather clearly from the remarks of the hon. member who introduced the bill what was intended, and that was my only purpose in asking the question.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question directed to me by the member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) as regards the amount of insurance which this company may undertake or which is now carried on by the company, section 7 (1) of the act provides that the company shall not commence any business of insurance until $250,000 of its capital stock has been bona fide subscribed. With regard to the amount of insurance that is already being done in this country, I am not in a position to say now how much is in force, but I would be prepared to have available for the hon. member in committee stage the amount of insurance that is now being carried.
With regard to the incorporators, it will be noted that all the incorporators reside in the city of Toronto. These gentlemen are also all solicitors, and I assume that I do not have to remind him that probably they are the original incorporators of the company. I am not able to give any undertaking as to whether they have or have not any shares in the English company. However, I think that, as solicitors, they are entitled to apply for incorporation. I hope that will be a sufficient answer to that question.

Mr. Speaker, once again I wish to oppose the enactment of this legislation designed to dissolve the marriage bonds and increase the number of divorces in Canada.
According to statistics that appeared in the newspapers recently, there are fewer divorces in Canada this year. Let us rejoice over the good news.
Our duty as members of parliament, however, consists in enacting legislation that is not at cross purposes with moral law. We must protect institutions considered sacred by the Catholic church, the United church and many others.
The rule decreeing that marriage is indissoluble may seem harsh, yet it was made in man's interest. It is the best ally and indispensable guardian of family happiness. It provides for a solid foafodation of the home, even before the house comes into being, since it leads those planning to marry to prepare for their future carefully.
The young man and the young woman who know that marriage is indissoluble, who have a sense of responsibility, do not doubt for an instant that marriage is something particularly great and important, to be entered into only after serious preparation.
At a time when the world is morally adrift, one has to be strong enough to go against the current. We must show ourselves fearless defenders of the family. Let our actions, and especially our legislation, impress upon those around us the greatness and beauty of Christian marriage. I believe that in doing so, we shall effectively promote the prosperity of the country, the happiness of our fellow countrymen and the salvation of their souls.

It is

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat has provoked my thoughts on this subject. He says he is opposed to divorce. So am I. But it is a rather peculiar situation to have the House of Commons constituted as the court of last instance which puts the final O.K. on divorce bills, accepting them like a pipe line-the whole stream of them-without ever having seen anything of the evidence, or examined it in any way, shape or form. Notwithstanding that fact, we are the people who say, in the final analysis, that these divorces are granted equally. I just cannot understand that situation.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), who wisely and courageously on many occasions rises in his place in this house and asks for the details of anything that affects the country, I think was well advised tonight when he stood up and said that at least these bills should be taken one at a time. If we have not the time to examine these bills, understand them, and make an intelligent decision on them, then we have not any right to have them here. In that connection, may I say that not so long ago there was introduced into this house a bill that had for its purpose the removal of divorce bills as such from the House of Commons and from the other place and the transferring of that responsibility not to a court in the province from which these bills come, and which is opposed to a divorce court, but to a federal court that is already established. If that were done, men who are trained in law and who understand this subject would be handling these bills and it would be done without the cost that there is today in connection with them. I think they could be handled much more cheaply in that way and without the undue publicity that there is now all through the country. This evidence goes out in book form. These cases make the best true stories that you could pick up. We argue in the house for that kind of thing, not because I believe in divorce- because I do not-but simply because I think it would make this matter much cleaner and would move it into a court administered by trained personnel, men who are better qualified than we are to make decisions.
I hate to sit in this house and be a member who accepts all of these bills en bloc and
Private Bills-Divorce
joins in putting the final O.K. of the House of Commons on them, when I have not seen the evidence and do not know whether or not these bills should be granted. For a time I served on the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills. When these bills would come before that committee I always objected to them on the grounds which the hon. member for Fraser Valley has stated. First, if there are children affected, they are the real sufferers. Second, in the province of Quebec where you can get a legal separation, if the parents are legally separated and neither is in a position to maintain the children or do not want to accept the responsibility, there are organizations which will look after the children. In some cases, however, when parents came before us we were told that this would be done as long as there was only a legal separation but that in the event of divorce these children were cut adrift, that the organizations then would not accept the responsibility for them. In many cases in which we are passing bills of this kind, we may be depriving children of the protection they are now receiving, in view of the fact that they will lose that protection in the event of a divorce being granted.
All of these things cannot be taken up, examined and decided on by laymen who merely take this business as an added responsibility and just get rid of it as fast as they can. This is a serious subject. You are dealing with the very foundation of the nation when you are dealing with family life. I still say that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was right; he is a minister of the church. While we may disagree with him in some things, I think we shall have to agree with the principle of the bill that he presented to the house for the purpose of placing this matter in legal channels, in the hands of people who are able to handle it properly, thus getting rid of the publicity that there is in connection with it at the present time and doing away with the possibility of collusion, manipulation and all that kind of thing that goes on under present circumstances.
I just wanted to make those remarks because I think the time has come when both the other place and the House of Commons will have to consider, more seriously than they have in the past, business such as we are transacting tonight.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the discussion so far has been all out of order. The last time when similar divorce bills were before the house-I think it was a week ago tonight- a similar debate took place. I drew to the

Private Bills-Divorce
attention of the Speaker-who at that time was not yourself-the fact that the debate was out of order. We are not debating the right of this parliament to deal with divorce cases. At the moment there is a particular point that you have to settle, namely, whether it is necessary, when an hon. member asks for it, that each bill be taken separately. But even if each bill is taken separately, such speeches as we have heard up to the present time are out of order.
Why?

Because the speeches did not deal with the principle involved in the bills before the house. It is not the principle of whether-as most hon. members say when they rise in their places-we are or are not in favour of divorce. Surely, it is a silly statement for anyone to make, and particularly for a member of parliament to make, that he is in favour of divorce. No one in his right senses is in favour of divorce?
Are you?
Wait a minute, and I will tell you whether I am in favour of divorce or not.
You are going to tell us, but you say it is a silly statement to make.

I say it is a silly statement for any member of this house to say that he is not in favour of divorce. I am not in favour of people divorcing each other just for the sake of divorcing each other. But I do believe, sir, it is the consensus in all of the civilized countries of the world-nearly all countries have divorce laws-that when two people cannot live together in harmony, each with respect for the other, it is not only desirable but it is the decent thing to let them separate. I cannot conceive of anything more indecent than for two people to live together in the intimacy of married life when the love and devotion that brought them together in the first place have disappeared. That is the way it appears to me, and to that extent I am in favour of divorce.
Now, sir, I am making a speech myself, and I am just as much out of order as the other hon. members were. 1 just wanted to draw a point of order to your attention- and perhaps we had better deal first with the point raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), whether you must, sir, at the request of any hon. member deal with each divorce case separately or, as we have always done, and as the custom has been for years, when a particular divorce case is not opposed, deal with them en bloc, because they have already been dealt with, not by people who do not know anything 
about legal procedure in those matters, but largely by lawyers who have become expert in dealing with divorce cases. I think, sir, that you should give your decision on the point raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley now.
What God has joined together.

As the hon. member for Vancouver East has said, it is not in order to discuss the principle of divorce generally on these bills. In my opinion the proper time to discuss that was when the bill to which the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred was before the house. The principle on which discussion can take place now is the principle involved in these bills, not on the question of divorce generally.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East has said, it has been the custom in this house to pass these bills by one motion, for the reason that the principle involved in all the bills is practically the same. It is true, as the hon. member for Fraser Valley has said, that in some instances there are children, and in other instances there are none. There is also the question which some hon. members may like to raise as to whether or not the party who has been wronged is being properly provided for. I do not know whether the act of parliament can do anything about that, but these matters can be considered in the committee on miscellaneous private bills to which these bills are referred.
As an hon. member has said, these cases have been considered in the Senate. After they receive second reading here, they are then referred to the committee on miscellaneous private bills, where the details on each case can be considered. I cannot rule that all the bills should be passed by one motion, unless the house so wishes me to do. I merely repeat that that has been the practice for a long time, but unless there is unanimous consent I will have to call the individual bills. Is it the pleasure of the house that I should call all the divorce bills which are on the order paper by one motion?
Yes.
Is it the pleasure of the house that the motion for second reading of these bills shall be adopted?
Yes.
No.

speechtext: On division.

Carried on division.
Motion agreed to on division, and bills read the second time.
The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Applewhaite for the second reading of Bill No. 116, respecting British Columbia Telephone Company.

Mr. Speaker, this bill to amend the charter of the British Columbia Telephone Company was last up for second reading on April 3. On that occasion I was able only to commence my remarks, and I am afraid I shall not be able to finish them this evening. However, I had pointed out that the Vancouver city council are opposing this bill on two grounds: in the first place on the ground that an excessive increase in capital is being sought by the company; and in the second place because under the present charter there is no protection against unreasonable charges being levied against the British Columbia Telephone Company by its parent and affiliated companies.
To deal with the question of the increase sought being excessive. In 1947, just four years ago, this company obtained an increase in capital from $11 million to $25 million. Of that total of $25 million, $5 million still remains in the treasury, although since I spoke early this month the $5 million in shares is being placed on the market. The company now asks for an increase from $25 million to $75 million, which of course would mean trebling the capital structure; if it is given this increase the result will be that in a period of four years the capital stock will have been increased sevenfold. As I said a moment ago, the company still has $5 million of the $25 million present capital; therefore, if there is the increase from $25 million to $75 million it will have available as share capital a total of $55 million unissued.
For many years they have been paying dividends of 8 per cent on their common shares. Now when they are planning to issue common shares we find that instead of getting $100 for those shares they are able to get $132.50. That means that on common stock issued at the present time and in the future they are able to get an extra third, approximately, over and above the face value of that stock.
Their published plans with regard to the $5 million in shares now in process of being issued are that $4 million is to be in common shares and $1 million in preferred shares. On the common shares now being issued the company will get $4 million, the face value, or the par value; and in addition will receive another $1,300,000, because these shares bring in $132.50 each.
British Columbia Telephone Company
Furthermore the present holders of common shares are getting share warrants which will give them the right to subscribe to these new shares now being issued on the basis of one new share for each two common shares held at the present time. On the other million dollars of the $5 million which, as I said, is being issued in the form of preferred shares, they will also get more than the face value of $100. They are receiving something like $102 per share.
So much for the capital; for that method of raising money for expansion-because, of course, the plea made for this increase is that the money is needed for purposes of expansion. But the practice of the company in financing has been not to rely upon shares alone, but to finance only to the extent of approximately 40 per cent by way of shares, and to raise the other 60 per cent by way of bonds and similar securities. So that if the company gets $55 million in share capital to use, it will be able to raise, on the 40/60 basis, an additional $82,500,000 by way of bonds. If this present increase in share capital is granted, this will give a possible $137,500,000 for expansion, plus the premiums on the shares to which I have referred, plus a very large depreciation reserve amounting to approximately $17 million at the end of 1950. So that the company will have available for expansion purposes over $150 million.
Let us look at the requirements. The sponsor of the bill said the company would require about $10 million a year for a period of ten years. Even if that is so, it means that with this increase the company will have sufficient money for at least fifteen years. But the company itself, at a hearing before the board of transport commissioners last year when consideration was being given to an application for an increase in telephone rates, said that its expansion program would be lasting until 1952, which is next year. And just a little over two weeks ago, at a hearing before the board of transport commissioners held here in Ottawa for permission to issue the five million in shares to which I referred, we find that counsel for the company said, as reported in a press dispatch of April 4, that the funds were to be used as part of an expansion program stretching into 1953- which is a matter of only two more years.
Nothing at all is said about an expansion program for a period of ten years.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

As a matter of fact even in 1949 and 1950 the company spent only approximately $8 million per year.

The Budget-Mr. McLure

I should like to ask the
hon. member a question, because I know he has no desire to create a false impression. Was not the expansion program to 1952, to which the hon. member refers, the program referred to in the house in 1947 when the original $20 million was asked for?

In any event, I do not believe the company will be able to spend $10 million a year for the next ten years. Much of the expansion has been caused by the installation of automatic telephones, and at least in the city of Vancouver that work will soon be completed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We hope so.

Furthermore, because of the shortage of material I do not believe it will be possible to get sufficient equipment to carry on an expansion program amounting to anything like $10 million a year. I believe if given the increase for which it is asking, the company will have enough for the next twenty years.
This would mean that parliament would have no check on the company for a period of twenty years. And remember, Mr. Speaker, that the necessity for the company to come before parliament fairly frequently has a salutary effect. It influences policy; it makes the officials more careful of the way they treat the public. I believe they fear having to come to parliament more than they fear making an application before the board of transport commissioners. In my view it would be a tragedy if the company were given an increase so large that it would not have to come back to parliament for a period of twenty years.
That is the first point upon which the city is protesting. I have not the time tonight to develop the second point which, as I said, is the need for protection against unreasonable charges by the parent and affiliated companies of the British Columbia Telephone Company. I shall deal with that when the bill comes up again.
On motion of Mr. Green the debate was adjourned.
It being nine o'clock, the house will resume the business which was interrupted at six o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house recessed at six o'clock I had been dealing with some matters which were of vital importance to my province of Prince Edward Island. I have only a few more subjects to discuss, and I shall be as brief as possible in doing so.
The first matter is one that I know will please the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) because, if carried into effect, it will show an annual saving for the government and the department presided over by the minister. This matter has to do with maritime freight rates. The estimates contain a large sum of money for maritime freight rates.
I wish these fellows would do their gossiping some place else, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know whether they have the floor or whether I have. If they do not want to stay inside there is plenty of room outside. I was about to say that the Maritime Freight Rates Act has been misunderstood not only by members of parliament but by many people outside the house. It is looked upon as, and sometimes is stated as being, a subsidy to the maritime provinces. The Maritime Freight Rates Act of 1927 was brought into effect to equalize freight rates in the maritime provinces compared with those of the western provinces, and also through rates from the maritime provinces to the west. From 1912 to 1926 freight rates were increased on a basis of 92 per cent in the maritime provinces against 55 per cent over all in the western provinces.
When the Sir Andrew Rae Duncan commission made an examination of the claims of the maritime provinces one recommendation made for the benefit of the farmers was that a 20 per cent reduction be made in the freight rates they paid to bring in feed grain and other freight to the maritime provinces for the benefit of the agricultural producers. Therefore it was not a subsidy but an equalization, or an endeavour to equalize, by lowering freight rates in the maritimes so that they would be more equitable compared with those in other parts of Canada. This was of great benefit to the maritime agricultural producers. I do not know the exact amount of the benefit to Prince Edward Island, but I know it would be quite large because our farmers are large buyers of feed grain from western Canada.
My proposition is a repetition of what has already been said to the government. I

suggest that the government should build an elevator at Charlottetown so that freight might come by water from Churchill to Charlottetown, be stored in the elevator and then distributed to our farmers as required. It would mean a large saving annually. I would say without fear of contradiction that it would save the government at least a million dollars annually and give better satisfaction to the agricultural producers of Prince Edward Island. I am not going into the details of the elevator that we hope will be built as has been promised to us. The matter has been placed before the government on several occasions, and I know very well that it will be of great benefit to our farmers. It will be appreciated by them, and all the maritime provinces will support it in parliament.
Furthermore, members from the vicinity of Churchill will also give it their fullest support. If it is possible to do so at all, I would plead with the government to give the matter the fullest consideration at this time having regard to what it will do for the maritime provinces, particularly Prince Edward Island, if the elevator is built, and the great benefit it will be to our agricultural producers.
