speechtext:
I am sure of that. Another problem that has been laid at our door recently with which I want to deal has to do with transportation. I might say that transportation is vital to any island province such as ours, and the same will be said later on of the island province of Newfoundland. The problem with respect to Prince Edward Island to which I wish to refer is not of our own making. Canadian National Railways have condemned the Hillsboro bridge leading from Charlottetown to Southport, a distance of a mile. I am sure that when they condemned it they must have had something else in mind in order not to shut off all traffic from Charlottetown to the southern part of the island. True, we have another way of shipping our freight, a detour from Charlottetown to Murray Harbour which is a much longer route. Passengers coming from Murray Harbour to Charlottetown, a distance of fifty-six miles, can come as far as the bridge to Southport. Then they have to get out of the cars, walk the rest of the distance, hire a taxi or get a bus in order to travel to the city of Charlottetown.
I mention the matter at this time because I understand that Canadian National Railways are negotiating with the government of Prince Edward Island. It is a proper time for these negotiations to go on because when the trans-Canada highway is being built that will be the time to rebuild the Hillsboro bridge from Charlottetown to Southport. It was an old bridge that was finished in 1904. As I have said before in this housfe, the top part of the bridge was fifty years old before it came to us, having been brought from the Miramichi river. However, it stood the test up until the present time. Now we expect that the Canadian government through the Canadian National Railways will build a new bridge there. With the completion of the trans-Canada highway they must cross in the region of the Hillsboro bridge at some point to go to the terminal of the line and also to connect with the Wood Island-Caribou ferry. I will leave that matter with the government but I did wish to draw it to their attention at this time.
Having mentioned those problems I have one more, in connection with the fisheries and fishermen of Prince Edward Island. During a storm last autumn the breakwater at the best fishing port in Prince Edward Island, namely North Rustico, was badly damaged. That breakwater is the only protection we have for the processing plants, the fishing plants and the homes of the fishermen. Had the storm not subsided just when it did all those plants and homes, as

The Budget-Mr. McLure well as the two range light, would have been carried out to sea. Kind Providence was good to us and the storm subsided, but it left the breakwater in a very dilapidated condition. Some 150 feet were carried away, and the rest was left in bad shape. Now the government are looking it over to see what can be done, and I understand some work has commenced already. I would suggest that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) get in touch with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and have this harbour thoroughly inspected from the point of view of what will be of lasting benefit to the fishermen of this port. I need say no more on that matter, but I do hope consideration will be given the interests of those people. I understand from fishermen who have spent their lives there that the work being undertaken now will not be satisfactory. They are afraid the tides may be somewhat altered and that as a result the harbour will be filled with silt and sand. Even today it is hard enough for the boats to get to and from the fishing grounds. I hope both departments will take this matter into consideration.
In the few moments remaining at my disposal I want to mention one other matter, and I shall be very brief. I refer to the mail carriers in Charlottetown in my constituency and the mail couriers in Queens county. The new regulations brought in by the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) have worked a great hardship upon these most faithful public servants. Under the new regulations, which were put into force with the idea of saving a few dollars, the position of the mail carrier has been affected for the worse. I had a letter from one of them today who says he is now compelled to serve 600 boxholders or residents of the city whereas previously he had to serve only 430. There is just one delivery a day, of course; but because of the large quantity of mail that must be handled these men have to go to work at 6 or 6.30 in the morning and are not through until 4.30 or 5 o'clock in the afternoon. In addition no recognition is given for the number of years they have served. Many of these men are veterans of the first war. The man from whom I had the letter today says that with the extra ground he has to cover and the extra mail he has to carry he finds it very difficult to continue his work from day to day.
As far as the rural mail couriers are concerned, the government has adopted a method under which they try to force down all tenders to the lowest possible figure. They call for tenders. After they are received those tendering get back a letter saying, "We find your tender rather high. Can you reduce

it?" I always understood that when tenders were called and opened, if the sureties were satisfactory the lowest tender would be accepted. Today very few mail couriers in my province, and particularly in my constituency, are even making a living wage when you consider their taxes and expenses. These men are becoming dissatisfied, and I do not wonder at it. At the same time I must say that our city mail carriers and country mail couriers are the finest class of individuals in Canada. If the department were so eager to make a saving I think they might have started with the top salaries instead of with the lower ones. I am sure that if even a small cut had been made at the top it never would have got down to the low brackets, because the objective would have been gained long before that. But it is always the same old story; when any economies are to be effected the department begins with the lower paid individuals. This does not make for good citizenship, because it breeds discontent among those people. I hope the Postmaster General will not carry this too far, because even now you hear things said that could not be placed on record because they are hardly parliamentary.
I see my time has almost expired, and in closing I want to make just one statement. In view of the facts I have brought forward this evening I believe it is my duty to insist and demand that our province be treated fairly and squarely. I know the people of Prince Edward Island would not desire me to beg, or to ask for any favours or handouts from the government. They do expect me, however, as the elected representative of both Liberals and Progressive Conservatives in my riding, to demand just and fair treatment, and the implementation of all the promises that have been made to my province. So I will demand that the federal government fulfil its pledges, political and otherwise, as well as the terms of confederation, as long as I am a representative from Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
in rising to take part in this budget debate, my first words must be those of commendation and appreciation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who for the past three or four years has carried on faithfully and earnestly in his duties as supervisor of the financial structure of this country. I would be remiss if I did not mention his parliamentary assistant, who has given him a great deal of assistance in the matters which he has carried out.
The budget which was brought down by the minister a few days ago I find has been accepted by the people of Canada. The

people of Canada are aware of the serious international situation with which we are confronted. They are ready to submit themselves to the additional taxes which must be levied upon them in order that the preparedness program may be met by the federal treasury. Even though we have before us at all times the serious international question, I believe that we should not lose sight of certain domestic problems which we have in this country. It will be my purpose tonight to point out to this house, and to other legislative bodies, a serious domestic problem which is the concern of the constituency I represent. I refer to the great menace of erosion.
In speaking on this particular subject, I ought to point out the geographical location of the constituency of Lincoln. We are the greater part of the Niagara peninsula, bounded on the north by lake Ontario, on the east by the Niagara river, on the west by the county of Wentworth, and on the south by the great industrial county of Welland and the Niagara escarpment. The county of Lincoln is a rich alluvial plain which slopes from the Niagara escarpment towards lake Ontario. In addition to the great industrial city of St. Catharines, we have the fertile lands which abound in this area. The farmers of our area cultivate the best peaches, pears, cherries, grapes and vegetables grown in the Dominion of Canada. However, they depend to a large extent on the products of the soil for their livelihood. It is an intensively cultivated area, and constitutes the major fruit and vegetable growing area of the province of Ontario.
Lake Ontario is the smallest of the great lakes, having a total water surface of about 7,500 square miles. Its length, from Burlington to the easterly end near Kingston, is 193 miles, and it has a breadth of 53 miles. The easterly portion of the south shore of the lake is exposed to northerly winds. A prominent cliff occurs along much of the shore, having a height of some 20 to 30 feet which gradually decreases to the west and gives way to a sandy shore. The water level of lake Ontario has been increased to some extent in the last ten years, owing partly to the fact that two diversions have occurred in lake Superior for the purpose of developing power. One of the diversions is referred to as the Ogoki diversion, and the other is the Long Lac diversion.
At these two points additions of water are permitted to go into the great lakes system, which has the effect of raising the water level of lake Ontario about 4 inches. I am told that the full effect of these diversions will not be felt on the great lakes until
The Budget-Mr. Cavers about 1956. It is true that some water is abstracted from the great lakes system at two points, Chicago and Tonawanda. The Chicago drainage canal, built about 15 or 20 years ago, takes some water from the great lakes system and lowers the level of lake Ontario by about 1-8 inches. The New York state canal, which diverts about 100 cubic feet per second, takes water from the Niagara river at Tonawanda but returns it again by way of the Genesee river near Buffalo, so the difference in the supply of water at this point is relatively negligible. However, we have placed a gut dam in the St. Lawrence at the head of the Galop rapids and the flow of water from lake Ontario has been retarded to some extent which has the effect of raising the water level by another 5 inches.
These mechanical changes are not the only factors which raise the water level, as additional height is given by reason of evaporation and precipitation. This gradual rise in the water level has a tendency to bring about a resultant wave of destruction which has caused the banks of lake Ontario to recede to a considerable extent. I am most concerned with that part along the southern shore of lake Ontario. In 1949 a survey was conducted by Dr. G. B. Langford, professor of mining and geology at the university of Toronto. This work was undertaken with the approval of the department of planning and development of the province of Ontario. Dr. Langford has published his report, which I have before me, dated May 1, 1949. It sets forth the rate of recession along the shore line of the southern part of lake Ontario. I refer to Dr. Langford's report and deal specifically with the townships, proceeding easterly from the Niagara river inward towards the city of Hamilton.
In Niagara township, the shore line from November, 1935, to December, 1949, has receded at the rate of 4 [DOT] 7 feet per year. In the township of Grantham in the period between September, 1936, and November, 1946, the shore line has receded 5-9 feet per year. For the township of Louth, the recession has been to a lesser degree. From December, 1922, to April, 1942, it was at the rate of 3-5 feet per year. By a reference to this report it will be noted that the easterly twelve miles of the shore line has been receding at the rate of 5 feet per year. There has been a loss along the other end of the peninsula of about 6 feet per year, or a loss of 3 acres of land per year over a period of five years. You may say that 13 acres is a relatively small thing, but in the 160 years during which farm operations have been carried on in the Niagara peninsula, there has been a loss of

The Budget-Mr. Cavers 2,000 acres of land, 13| square miles of valuable, arable land. There are farmers who state that they have lost one or more rows of fruit trees in a period of five years. As the population of our country grows there will be an increased demand for the type of farm produce that can be grown only in our particular area. It is imperative that we should protect every square foot of it. It is a limited national asset which, once gone, cannot be replaced.
There are those who, by individual effort, have endeavoured to solve this problem. Some individuals along the shore line have endeavoured to erect breakwaters and have deposited rock in order to erect groins jutting out into the lake. Their efforts have been rewarded to some extent. Where this work has been done, you will see small promontories extending out into lake Ontario. Then there were others who banded themselves together in an association known as the Ontario Shore and Beach Preservation Association.
The object of this association was to urge upon governments the formulation of a plan to combat the serious menace of erosion in the province of Ontario. The association did not pick out any particular area. Being a province-wide association, it was necessary that they should commence and continue their work on a province-wide basis. But their work was not in vain, for they were successful in obtaining the report of a special select committee on conservation in the province of Ontario; they also have for their efforts the report which I have read, undertaken by Dr. Langford. The opinion seems to have become more prevalent of late that this matter is not one for the individual but rather is one of public responsibility. A project of this kind to save the shore line and particularly valuable lands in this area should not be undertaken by the individual but is a matter for collective work. It is a public responsibility. Dr. Langford in his report has recommended that there should be placed out in the lake, groins which would tend to collect sand deposits about them and produce a wider sandy beach.
I think that the time is opportune for work of this kind to be undertaken in our particular area. The Niagara power diversion plan is about to be commenced by the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission. In commencing this work they will endeavour, within the next few months, to develop an open cut extending from Chippawa north through the Niagara escarpment and opening again on the Niagara river at Queenston. This would seem to be a most advantageous time 1o commence work of this kind.

I would suggest-and such suggestions have been made to the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission that they should provide the rock for an undertaking of this kind. There is a local rumour to the effect that the rock may be dumped on valuable lands in the area. I hope that this rumour is not well-founded, because such action would ruin many of the valuable lands in that particular area. The Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission have done something to provide additional beauty for their power house at Queenston, in the establishment of the finest floral clock on the North American continent. I would hope that they would not with the one hand build up an edifice of this kind and with the other hand wipe out that advantage by destroying the landscape of the lands in our particular area. Furthermore, they would save investment in lands required for this purpose. In the course of my remarks I shall not attempt to assess the cost of such an undertaking. It would be ridiculous for me to attempt to assess costs of this kind because in this day of fluctuating prices and increasing costs any such attempt would have but little meaning. I propose, however-and such proposals would be made-that the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario might donate the rock. I urge upon the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) that the federal government should assume 25 per cent of the cost of this undertaking. I also urge upon the provincial government of Ontario that 25 per cent of the cost should be assumed by them. The adjoining townships or municipalities have already intimated that they are prepared to contribute 25 per cent of the cost; and the owners of adjoining lands on the lakefront have already undertaken and agreed to supply the remaining 25 per cent of the cost of this work.
Some years ago the government of the United States recognized the problem of erosion. By public discussion results have been obtained in the formulation of policies which will deal with this problem. European countries on the north Atlantic and on the North sea, for some years "have been fighting the eroding seas". I think that we in Canada must accept this public responsibility, and that this is a most opportune time to make a beginning on the south shore of lake Ontario.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as one who has not much time for the repetition which takes place in this house, I find myself at a loss for words this evening. I might say that the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Cavers) has practically taken the words out of my mouth.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then say, "me too."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is not a new subject with me. I have brought it to the attention of this house on one or two occasions previously. I must compliment the hon. member for Lincoln for making a fine presentation of this problem which is of great concern to the counties of Lincoln and Wentworth and to other adjoining properties. At a meeting of the Lake Shore Erosion Conference, held in Toronto in March, 1948, the following resolution was passed:
Resolved that this organization ask the provincial and federal governments to instruct their engineeers to make a survey of the erosion on the great lakes and report with a recommendation for a remedy; and in this report be included a report on the effects of the Ogoki and Albany river diversions on the level of the great lakes.
While this resolution went forward at that time to the Ontario government and to the federal government, the latter have disclaimed any knowledge of ever having received it. As has just been said by the hon. member for Lincoln, however, the Ontario government appointed Mr. G. B. Langford, and he made a survey and a report several years ago. I have always claimed that the federal government should assume a portion of the responsibility because it was only a few years ago that a former premier of Ontario approached the federal government and persuaded them to legalize the diversion of waters from the Ogoki and Albany rivers into the great lakes system which means, as the hon. member for Lincoln has just said, that there is flowing into the great lakes system some 1,700 cubic feet per second of additional water that formerly flowed towards James bay and the Arctic circle. It is argued by many engineers that this diversion had a great deal to do with the higher levels that we have experienced during the past several years.
In the immediate vicinity of Hamilton beach and Van Wagner's beach just a few months ago they experienced a great deal of trouble, and many houses have been practically washed away. The common answer to that is: Well, they should not have built so near the shore line. In many instances the older houses that were built years ago were built a considerable distance from the shore line at that time, but because of this constant erosion, in some instances up to six and often nearly seven feet a year over the past fifteen or twenty years, the shore line has receded upwards of 200 feet. A serious condition is facing the people in the Niagara peninsula.
As I said on one other occasion, if the two governments, the federal and provincial, do not stop passing the buck, and get together
The Budget-Mr. Lennard and do something on this matter, the great Niagara fruit belt will pass out of existence in a few years.
In that connection the United States policy was slow to develop in the beginning, but it is quite definite today. In 1929 the problem was formally recognized by the establishment in the corps of engineers of a departmental board on sand movement and beach erosion. This was followed the next year by the creation of the United States beach erosion board of four officers of the corps of engineers and three civilians. The board was originally authorized only to make studies and investigations of erosion problems in co-operation with state governments, and the expenses of such investigations were to be shared by the two governments.
The duties of the board were expanded, however, in 1945 and it was authorized to act independently of state governments in studying shore erosion; while at the same time being able to act with them if asked to do so. The state governments were no longer asked to share the cost of such investigations. As an evidence of a growing sense of federal responsibility in this matter, the board was asked to make specific recommendations on what share of the expenses of recommended shore protective works should be borne by the federal government.
The following year, the central government's willingness to share in the cost of protective works was stated as follows:
It is hereby declared to be the policy of the United States to assist in the construction, but not the maintenance, of works for the improvement and protection-of the shores-that are owned by states, municipalities or other political subdivisions.
The existing policy in the United States can be summed up as follows:
1.	The federal government is prepared to make studies of shore erosion and recommendations for protective works on any shore property, whether publicly or privately owned. This may be done in co-operation with state governments or independently of them.
2.	The federal government is also prepared to assist in the construction of protective works for property that is publicly owned, up to one-third of the total cost of such works.
3.	The federal government will not assist in the maintenance or repairs to existing structures, except in the case of protection of important highways.
It is quite evident that the United States government recognizes the seriousness of the erosion that is taking place on our great lakes in connection with property over which they have control. The federal government should seriously consider taking such

The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray measures as would set up machinery to do likewise in Canada. The suggestions made by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Cavers) that the municipalities, provincial and federal governments, share the cost is certainly commendable.
Just a word on the budget; it has been pretty well covered, and as I said earlier this evening, and as I have said on other occasions, I am not one who believes in repetition in this house-we hear so much of it and it is so tiring. What I have to say, while it will be repeating what other members have said, will yet take only a few minutes, and therefore I feel it will not cause too much hardship on some of the hon. members who are so patient and who sit here for many hours listening to this tiresome repetition.
X cannot understand why electric stoves, washing machines and refrigerators were picked out as luxury items, and liquor was considered a necessity. I am absolutely opposed to the increase in the sales tax. I am opposed to a sales tax of any kind, and always have been. I say that, knowing who was responsible for introducing the sales tax in this country. I have always been opposed to it. It is an unjust tax. I do not believe in hidden taxes-goodness knows we have too many of them. If the people of this country knew just how heavy the hidden taxes were we would have a revolution.
To begin with, any sales tax should be visible, not hidden. If the minister hopes, as he says he does, to keep down inflation by discouraging spending, then, by having a hidden sales tax he will not achieve that result; but if the sales tax were visible people would be discouraged from buying many articles that they buy today. I know that is a fact today because I have been in other countries where they have a visible sales tax. In fact I have been in some provinces of this country where they had a visible tax, and it rather irritated me a bit, and when I was about to buy an article with an additional tax on it I said: "You can keep it"; and I went off without it.
In closing I may say that this sales tax, with its increase, is in my opinion one of the most stupid taxes to have inflicted on the country at this time. If a sales tax is to be applied it certainly should not be applied to what I consider necessities, absolute necessities to people in the lower income brackets, people with large families who have to pay so much for the clothing they require. They should not have to pay these multiple taxes to secure these necessities.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from the great dairying county

of Oxford, I think I should use first of all, in appreciation of the warmth of the applause tonight, the reply that the Oxford county cow is reported to have given a kind lady on a cold frosty morning, namely, thank you for the warm hand.
I should like to say also that as the member for Oxford I would want to join in the sentiments that were conveyed here this week by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank), namely, words of appreciation to the Speaker of this house, who comes from the city of Brantford, a city close to my home, and say also to you, sir, it is my hope that you may long be spared to add lustre and distinction to this assembly and to confer upon this chamber the benefit of your wisdom and of your talents.
Likewise I should like to join tonight in this, my maiden speech before the house, in a word of appreciation to the one who today leads this nation of Canada, the revered and respected leader of the government, the Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, and to say to him that, just as mothers of men rejoice in the achievements and accomplishments of honoured sons, and not less for those achievements than for those qualities which endear them to their fellow men, so too, in turn tonight, do we pay tribute to the Prime Minister of Canada-not less for his achievements, not less for all his accomplishments in the legal world than for those innate qualities of kindness and of friendship and of integrity and of character which have endeared him to all the people of this nation.
I am reminded, sir, that it is neither wealth nor riches that brings greatness to an institution, yea even to the House of Commons, but it is the men and the women who travel in its service. And so tonight I am proud to be associated with hon. members of the house who are giving of their time and of their talents for the betterment of a better Canada, and for the betterment of our citizens.
It seems to me, sir, that if a man tries to do the job he has set out to do, and does that job faithfully, efficiently and well, even though he be a humble member of the house, a backbencher, he is serving Canada just as efficiently and just as well as those in higher positions. I can realize that that may find reluctant resistance in the minds of some at this time. I hasten to say I am not thinking of the grand eloquence surrounding us, or of the magnitude of the task. I am thinking of the soul and life of Canada. And so again I say I am proud to be associated with the membership of the house

who are giving of their time, of their ability and talents for the betterment of the citizens of today.
After all, the quality of a nation is nothing more and nothing less than the quality, integrity and character of its people, and of those who manage its affairs. I think it was Schiller who once remarked that an artist is judged, not by what he places on canvas but rather by what he leaves out. I hasten to say tonight that I make no claim to artistic genius or eloquence. It is because of the repetition that has already taken place in this debate that I must, of necessity, eliminate a great deal that already has been said.
However if I should be halting in my words or in expressing my thoughts I know hon. members will not judge me insincere when I join my voice with the many who have already spoken in commendation of the Minister of Finance for the straightforward and businesslike manner in which he has approached this year's budget. The very reason for having a part in Canada's parliament is to make some contribution to the preservation of Canada's democracy. It seems to me that the very foundation of democracy lies in voluntary co-operation and the preservation of personal liberty.
These are days, we recognize, when men are assailing the ideals of democracy, not only in those countries which are distinctly antidemocratic; in our own country there are some who are saying that democracy has failed, and that we should replace it with some other type of autocratic control. My own ambition for the rest of my life, and for whatever influence I may have in the public affairs of this nation, is to make some contribution to the preservation of Canadian democracy.
I do not say that tonight in any vainglorious spirit, nor for the purpose of making myself feel superior; but because of our natural surroundings, because of the great natural resources of our dominion, and because of the splendid parent stock that is to be found in the old races of Canada. In that heritage I feel rests the inspiration which makes possible an even higher and finer contribution to Canada today than we have hitherto dreamed of.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that in this debate one is privileged to tell something of his constituency. With the poet tonight I can easily say that-
The sea hath its pearls The sky hath its stars But my heart hath love-
2G, 1951
The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray -a love for Oxford, and its people. Born within its boundaries, as I was, and having lived there all my life, I have come to know and to appreciate the wondrous heritage of the hospitality of its people.
While I have listened to many members within this chamber tell of the greatness of their constituencies, one's heart naturally yearns for his native riding. With due apologies to Robert Burns tonight I fain would say:
The bridegroom may forget his bride,
Who married was but yesterday;
The mother may forget her child.
Who sleeps so sweetly on her knee;
The king he may forget his crown That on his head the hour hath lain
But I will not thou-
Oxford-
-forget
For a' that thou hast been to me.
So I say to you tonight that while others have mentioned the greatness of their constituencies, this evening I choose to kodak, to develop and to print one of the finest counties in the Dominion of Canada, the finest flower in the garden, the first prize chrysanthemum, the county of Oxford in the province of Ontario.
Last week while I was home I heard my mother retell the story of how my grandparents came from the land of Scotland, taking as many weeks to cross the Atlantic as it now takes days. I heard her tell of how, around my home city of Woodstock, which in those days was bush and forest, with only a trail through the woods, by industry and hard work the trees were felled, the log cabins built and the soil tilled.
Oxford is famous for its Scotch ancestors, and has given many men to all branches of life-men who have given everything to take their places in the professional, the commercial and the industrial life of the nation. Born in humble homes, reared midst hardships and want, at times, unconsciously they were trained by a stern but kind Providence in those habits of economy, of temperance and of hard work which have later brought them to the fore in all departments of life.
I think it was Emerson who wrote that the true test of civilization is not the size of the cities or the population, but rather the kind of men a country turns out. And tonight, in passing, I shall mention only Ralph Connor, known to many because of his writings, and particularly his book "The Man from Glengarry." I would mention likewise the late Dr. George Leslie McKay, the well known missionary to Formosa.
I would pause briefly to pay tribute to the township of my birth, the township of Zorra

The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray in the county of Oxford. I cannot think of any finer honour Oxford county cherishes today than this, that it is the birthplace of an honoured colleague in the House of Commons, the genial member for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross), and likewise the birthplace of my honoured colleague and namesake, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray), whose mother, whose brothers and whose sisters are deeply respected citizens of my native Oxford.
Likewise as a native of Zorra I am sure my honoured colleague would join me tonight in the lines reported as having been said by a lady at the time of the Fenian raid in Zorra:	They may take Montreal, they may
take Ottawa, they may take Toronto, but they will not take Zorra. So I say to you this evening that Oxford is noted for its prosperity, for its quiet beauty of rolling hills, of well cultivated fields, its gentle streams and its friendly people. Nestled within its boundaries are the towns of Inger-soll, Tillsonburg, Tavistock, and my own home city of Woodstock, ofttimes called the city beautiful or the industrial city, indicative of the long rows of maple trees which adorn our city streets and the initiative and enterprise of our people. Situated as it is in a very prosperous section of Ontario, it has shared in the general prosperity which our nation has enjoyed, and my fondest wish tonight as I take my stand on behalf of my people is that it may continue to share for many years to come that prosperity which has enriched it in days gone by.
Taking my stand tonight on behalf of the constituency of Oxford, I am reminded that it has been represented by a number of illustrious men including the late Sir Francis Hincks, the Hon. George Brown, Thomas Oliver, the late Hon. James Sutherland, Dr. Sinclair, A. S. Rennie, and in more recent times, the Hon. D. M. Sutherland, formerly minister of national defence, my predecessor, Mr. K. R. Daniel, and others, who in the past have given to this assembly the benefit of their wisdom and their talents, and have truly lent lustre and distinction to it. Tonight as I think of that long line of illustrious men, and while I realize that imperfections no doubt may follow tonight, I want to present some thoughts particularly as they pertain to this year's budget.
I want to say first of all that one could be alarmed at the amount that is to be appropriated for the defence of our nation. I think, however, that we all must realize the situation in the small atomic world wherein we live, but I would not want to be an alarmist. I would not want to wave any flags of undue patriotism or to be accused of speaking directly against the peoples of 
any nation because I do not think that the mass of the people of Russia want war any more than you or I or other nations throughout the world want war today. I think we all want peace but because of these fourteen or fifteen men in the Kremlin, because of their record of leadership, a leadership that cannot be trusted, there is no other course to follow than that which has been followed by the government of this nation, namely, to build its defences strong.
Therefore I say, and I am weighing every word as I say it this evening, that as of now the people of Canada must be prepared to build our defences strong. Without indicating that there will be any war, any atom bombs used, any germicidal warfare, I think all hon. members must realize that we must put first things first, and by so doing I for one hope that the jet planes that are being built and the bombers that are being constructed will be the means not of winning world war III but rather of preventing it. Therefore I say tonight that while I realize it is not a very popular thing for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to come to the people of the country and say that large sums of money have to be appropriated for the defence of our land, on the other hand there is no other method to follow than that which has been followed, and which no doubt will be followed increasingly over the next number of months, the method of solidarity building for that day which we hope will come when the peoples of all nations will come to learn to live together in peace and harmony, and when those who have perverted ideas in places of leadership will finally be dethroned.
Turning from international relations to domestic affairs I want to bespeak at this time the appreciation of the profession to which I belong, the pharmaceutical associations throughout Canada, and the appreciation of all citizens, to the Minister of Finance for the exemption under the budget of special drugs the cost of which is deductible for income tax purposes. I should like to say to the Minister of Finance that while we appreciate that he has recognized this principle of deduction we hope in turn that he may see his way clear to add to it to include all medical prescriptions so that it may be of equal benefit to the citizens of the nation.
I should like to intimate that Oxford is also concerned about the transition that is taking place today in the agricultural life of the nation. I hope that even a preponderance of government members does not preclude my emphasizing within this chamber that agriculture should receive a most considered position. It is needless to repeat that a prosperous

agriculture means a prosperous Canada, that farm income is the keynote to national prosperity. I can personally vouch for the fact that when the farmer is prosperous, cash registers ring more merrily in the cities. I think we can pretty well all agree that agriculture and industry will rise and fall together. But what we must not forget is the importance of agriculture in the economy of the nation. Generally speaking, our farming people are ready to meet the contingencies of climate such as frost and snow, but I do not think they want their chins punched from all directions. Nor do they want a lot of government controls which would be the natural thing under subsidized farming.
Indeed I should like to commend the government for the position it has taken on controls. Controls do not cure inflation. They but contain it. At this time I want to commend the government for not putting the business economy of our nation in a strait-jacket where it would be subject to regimentation, to export and import controls, black markets and all the rest that goes with it. I should say to you, sir, that I am in the retail drug profession, and I went through the period when we had controls. I make bold to say that during the control period we were out of selling condition. You will remember we went quickly from an ordinary, very healthy, sane buyers' market into a sellers' market. It was not a question of getting customers or selling to them. The whole normal process of business was completely reversed. Let me give you a personal illustration. The retailer was not seeking customers. Rather customers were seeking the retailer. Similarly the wholesaler was not seeking the retailer. The retailer was seeking the wholesaler. As a personal illustration, I can say that when a traveller came into the store during the period of controls you went all out with him endeavouring to seek from him the goods that you so dearly desired. You would go up to him and say, "Here, sir, have a chair; have a cigar, have a stenographer"; anything to get out of him the goods you so badly needed. During that period we also had the rationing of goods. You could have some; I could not. That affected goods such as sugar, meat, rubber, gasoline, chocolates, and all the rest of it. I hope those days will not return.
The point I am endeavouring to make is that during that control period we were out of selling condition. Goods were hard to get; sales were easy to make, and as a result we became soft and inefficient. So let us be guided by that period. Let us keep those virtues of hard work, industry, enterprise, patience and persistence as the hall-marks of our national efforts in the days ahead.
20, 1951
The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray Let us hearken to the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who guided the productive energies of this country during the last war, and who has said that hard work, production and savings will bring us through this period of difficulty just as it did before. Let us pay heed to the words of the Minister of Finance, that it is an inexorable law of life that everything we get must be paid for. Freedom is not free; it was bought at a price, and we are going to have to pay the price to retain it.
I confess, sir, that when I hear the many requests for assistance that come from certain quarters of this chamber I become a little disturbed. It is not that we are not all anxious for the welfare of our fellow men, for old age pensions, health insurance and so on; but I become concerned that at the same time we do not kill by taxation the enterprise, initiative and industry which have made our nation what it is. I may be a little old fashioned in my thinking, but I still feel that those attributes of hard work, industry, production and saving are the beacon light in the destiny of Canada. Oft-times I feel that we are suffering from a disease in this land. It is not cancer; it is not polio; it is not heart disease. It is more insidious than any or all these. It so weakened one country that she was not able to defend herself in time of war. It is not the shortage of dollars; it is the shortage of work. Some people have fallen for the old idea, or the new idea, of shorter hours and more pay, when it seems to me that what is needed in Canada today is more work and more production to trade with the peoples of other countries. This week the house witnessed the spectacle of an hon. member rising in his place and piling high upon his desk volumes pertaining to the exuberant and vociferous demands made upon this government, demands that have to be paid for by the hard work and taxes of our people. Tonight I say to that hon. member that he omitted one book on that occasion, the most important book of all. I have that book with me; I have brought it from the hotel where I stay, where it was placed by the Gideons. I do not want to alarm hon. members but I do want to read the 19th verse of the 3rd chapter of Genesis, wherein it says:
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground.
That is God's law; it is nature's law; it is true, and immutable. How can anyone think he may change it? Unfortunately, however, there appear to be people going through our land, agitators, saying to young men and men who are not so young, "Do as little as you can; get as much as you can." I point out

The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray that this is contrary to those laws of virtue and industry that we learned at our mother's knee. We cannot hope to maintain the vigour and wealth of our country with any theory such as that. So to a certain section of this house I say that while some may sing siren songs of the pleasures of delight when we all receive more by doing less, tonight I bring a word that speaks for itself in this fashion. I am the foundation of all prosperity. I am the fount from which all blessings flow. I am the salt that gives life its savour. I am the friend of every young man and every young woman, and when he or she puts his or her hand in mine and keeps it there for a lifetime I will do more for that person than the richest parent. I am the sole support of the poor, and the rich who think they can get along without me lead ineffectual lives and fill premature graves. I have made this Dominion of Canada. I have laid its railways; I have paved its highways; I have set a standard of living unequalled in the world. What am I? I am work, the answer to this problem of inflation, the answer to the building up of the defences of this nation against any potential enemy of the future, the answer to the recreating of wealth destroyed by war, the answer to the building of a greater and finer Canada than hitherto we have known.
So I say to this chamber tonight, let us set the example in our own lives. Let us teach this to our children. If we pray, as I hope we all do, let us pray that management and labour may fuse their forces into a productive whole that will continue to build this great land with the same zeal and energy that the men and women of Canada have displayed in defending it. In this great land there is no other way for us to follow than to be constantly, continually, habitually and eternally optimistic regarding it. I recognize that there are some in the country who are apostles of doom and disaster, who can see nothing but trials and tribulations before us. Fortunately there are not many of that kind. We on the government side say the history of Canada has been made up of meeting challenges and difficulties, so the future is not going to frighten us provided we bring to it the industry, brains and initiative we all possess but may not be using to the full.
There is one thing more which was emphasized this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). The crying need of the world today is unity versus antagonism, co-operation against rivalry. Above all we need unity in spirit among the nations of the world. Today the privilege of being a Canadian carries with it a great

responsibility. A few years ago we were Upper and Lower Canada. Today we are one. Having done so much, is it not our duty to do more? The unifying power of our race is not exhausted. None can deny that in Canada we have enjoyed a period of prosperity unequalled in our history. As we face the future let us not forget that Canada's economic policy must march in step with the policies of those who are or may become our friends. It must be in the interests of Canada, but of a Canada which could not tonight, even if it wanted, remain isolated or insulated from the community of nations that today inhabit this small atomic world.
We must learn, Mr. Speaker, to get along together; to live together and to trade together. So, as I bring these remarks to a close, I wish to commend the government, our leader and our ministers, for the action that has been taken in building up the defence of our nation; in making our country strong; and likewise to emphasize that while we have these defence obligations we have other obligations to build somehow, some way, the attributes of decency among all peoples throughout the world and to work for that day when peace shall come and wars shall be no more.
May dishonour blast our names
And quench our household fires,
If we or ours fail this land.
This dear land of our sires.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too represent the best constituency in Canada. I want every member of this house to know that I shall not talk very long in this debate, but I thoroughly believe the arguments I shall presently advance. My remarks in English will be brief, because they are a summary of the more elaborate ones that I shall make in my own language. I request the indulgence of my Englishspeaking colleagues if some of my expressions sound queer and rather illiterate. It is due to my limited knowledge of your language. However, I shall do my best to be as clear as possible so that there can be no misinterpretation of my meaning.
During this speech I shall make some recommendations, and of course as I said my remarks will be longer in French than they will be in English. The main reason for my participation in this debate is to bring to the attention of the government the opinion of the average citizen, and his reaction to the proposed budget for the coming fiscal year, as well as the increased taxes it imposes. When I speak of the "average citizen" I mean the small merchant, the medium and low wage earner, who compose

the majority of those in the urban constituencies. In a democracy a good government, such as this one, must take note of public recommendations or expectations. The same principle applies to every member in a party. We all agree, Mr. Speaker, that the chief worry of the classes I mentioned a moment ago is the constant increase in the cost of living and the overcoming of this problem. Some serious minded people suggest that price control be imposed, while others are of the opposite opinion. I have already expressed my views on this subject. In my opinion price control cannot be exercised unless wage controls are also established. Wages cannot be frozen at their present rate, especially in the case of unskilled labour and the so-called white-collar workers, because in the majority of cases these workers do not earn enough to make both ends meet.
I am not the only member who is of this opinion. I listened with a great deal of interest to a speech made by the member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) the other day, in which he said the following, as it appears on page 1751 of Hansard of April 9, 1951:
You cannot have price control unless you also have wage control.
On the same page the hon. member says:
Does anyone in the house want control now all across the board on all commodities, control that will affect our exports and imports? Certainly people are not ready for such a situation. I noticed that the amendment moved this afternoon by the leader of the opposition is well guarded in its language. You heard it, and I will read it again. It is as follows:
"This house is of the opinion that in view of the announcement made on Wednesday last of the greatest monthly increase in Canadian cost of living during the month of February to the disastrously high level of 179-7, immediate consideration should be given to the adoption of appropriate measures to hold down the cost of living and halt inflation."
The member for Cochrane added: "There is no mention of control there." The government, as well as everyone else, is well aware of the grave situation which is facing a large number of our citizens. I feel confident that every effort will be made to alleviate, as much as it is within the power of the government to do so, the privation encountered by so many people today. However, according to the declarations of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and other members of his cabinet, price controls are not advisable, for the very good reasons put forth in recent speeches.
I have heard a lot of criticism from members of the opposition. I have read thoroughly the address delivered by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), and scrupulously analysed the amendment he
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis has proposed. This amendment reads as follows, at page 2053 of Hansard of April 16, 1951:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"the proposals of the Minister of Finance are unsatisfactory because they will inevitably increase the cost of living for all and especially for those least able to bear it.
This house condemns in particular, as inflationary, the increase by 25 per cent of the general sales tax and is of the opinion that the increase is unnecessary and unwise.
This house further condemns the heavy increase in excise taxes on certain essential commodities and is of the opinion that much of the government's proposed huge increase in taxation is due to its own extravagance.
This house regrets the failure of the government to take effective steps to deal with profiteering."
According to the hon. member, who is known as the main financial critic of the official opposition, all the taxes imposed to meet the estimates of the coming fiscal year are too high and improperly applied. Has the hon. member, for whom I have the greatest respect, made any suggestions as to the sort of taxes that should be imposed, or on what category or group of people in particular the burden should be placed? The opposition is reproaching the government for the immensity of the taxes the Canadian people will have to pay. What would these taxes have amounted to if the government had listened to the screams of anguish of the opposition and adopted their suggestion for the immediate regimentation of the reserve forces? Such a measure would have considerably increased our war expenditures.
We are facing a crucial situation and nothing must be spared which will assure the survival of democracy. But we must pay for this, and taxes must be levied. We may consider ourselves fortunate that we have now at the head of the country leaders who have not been panic-stricken and who have acted wisely in adopting measures required by the times. Should they be forced to ask for more sacrifices from the people, I am sure that this government will take this responsibility at the proper time.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), in his remarks, made this statement as reported at page 2053 of Hansard:
I am not asking for a miracle. On the other hand negation is not a policy.
In this statement I agree with the hon. member. I would not dare to criticize the policy of anybody unless I had some better proposal to make. The remarks made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) himself are nearly all negative, as they contain only reproaches of the government or condemnation of their actions. The speeches of

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis members of the opposition in general contain no constructive recommendations.
Some say that it is the business of the government to settle the administrative problems of the country. I say that it is the business of every member of this house to make any suggestions that he may think are for the good of the country. As I said a little while ago, I am going to make some recommendations. It may be too late for them to be applied to the budget that is now receiving our attention; but at the same time I think there is ground for study of certain suggestions I will make. For instance, has the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) ever considered the advisability of imposing income taxes on profits made on some transactions, such as on the sales of businesses? There is now such a tax in the United States and it has given good results. I am thinking of the case of taverns changing hands two or three times during the same year, each owner realizing profits ranging from $20,000 to $50,000. Why not tax such income? It is a profit. It is an income, after all. Why not tax it at the source as is done in the case of all salaried 'people? The same remark would apply to stock market speculators. They could also be taxed at the source, by taxing them indirectly, through the services of the broker, on the profits they realize on certain transactions. Although as I said a little while ago it may be too late for these measures to be put into force for the coming fiscal year, I sincerely believe that if such measures were put into force the government would probably be in a position, if not to lower the present rate of income tax at least to keep it at the present rate and not increase it.
One must bear in mind the fact that the employee cannot escape the payment of his income tax, which is deducted at the source and reported to the authorities by the employers. It has not been done only under this government. It has been suggested, I suppose, by great economists. I know it is a good way of collecting income tax. I am not in favour of the worker escaping payment of income tax. I am not suggesting that at all. I am just pointing out the fact that there are, in a way, two kinds of treatment: one treatment for one class and another treatment for another class. When we can reach people through such business transactions as those I noted a little while ago, I think the proposal I made would be worthy of the attention of the government.
I hope the government will give immediate attention to the plight of the state pensioners, among whom I would include Canadian National railway ex-personnel and also-veterans. Every member of this house knows 
that these former employees cannot carry on and meet the actual cost of living with a pension that was fixed on the occasion of their departure several years ago.
I have a special recommendation of local or regional importance, namely, the abolition of the tolls on the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges, joining the south shore of the St. Lawrence river to the city of Montreal. The city of Montreal and the province of Quebec have already paid large sums to cover the yearly deficits, and I think it is now time to render justice to the citizens of this part of the country, especially those residing on the south shore, whose numbers have grown so rapidly in the last decade. I consider that the toll charged to them is discriminatory in a way, in view of the fact that in no other place in the province of Quebec is a passage fee collected for travelling on bridges. Some of the residents on the south shore are using the bridge several times a week, and some even use it many times every day; and I think that this is a kind of indirect tax which is charged them.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, this is a summary in the language spoken by the majority of the members of this house. Before I finish my remarks in that language I want to say this. I would have given my serious attention to any proposal coming from any side of this house and tending to improve the present situation. I am not going to vote for the amendment, as it contains no such suggestions but rather merely expressions of blame against this government. As I said previously, although the situation in some quarters, in constituencies such as the one I have the honour to represent, is not flourishing, nevertheless it is not desperate. It is certainly different from that which existed in the thirties. I was an alderman at that time and a member of the executive of the city of Montreal.
They are not very particular in choosing their executive members there. In any event,
I was a member of the executive for two terms and alderman for five terms. I went through the period of depression, and I saw a great deal of misery. I saw people almost dying of hunger, I would say. I have seen landlords receiving direct relief. I have seen business people getting out of business owing to the depression. Some people are trying to replace the word "depression", are trying to frighten us with that word "inflation", and are comparing the situation we have today with that of the thirties. At that time, with a budget of $55 million, the share of the city of Montreal for direct relief alone was $1,500,000 a month; and I repeat that this

was just enough to save people from starving. But when we compare the situation today and we see the prosperity around us everybody will note the facts. Look at the provincial budget. I am thinking of the budget of my own province. At the time I am speaking of now, around 1935 and 1936, that budget was somewhere around $55 million. It is now over $200 million. Well, if that is a sign of depression-I know I am not an economist- but if this is not the sign of some prosperity, I do not understand the first word about business.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It may be a sign of inflation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be a sign of inflation; it may be a sign of prosperity. If inflation exists today in some proportion I hope the time will change and that prosperity will come again, as I am quite sure that the present government-as they have always done-will take the necessary precautions to see that prosperity will be assured in the future. Mind you, I am not trying to get in the good graces of the government at the present time. I am simply expressing sincerely what I believe to be the right thing.
Taking into account the efforts madie by the present government to overcome this difficult situation, I do not hesitate to give all my confidence to the cabinet, and by doing so I am reflecting, I am quite sure, the opinion of those whom I have the honour to represent in this house.
(Translation):
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I am not one of those who spend their time criticizing the actions of our government without even offering suggestions calculated to improve present conditions or any other situation. As was so well pointed out by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the opposition goes so far as to brand even our best as very wrong.
I know perhaps better, at least as well as any other member of this house, the hardships that some of our people have to put up with, and there is not a shadow of a doubt that those new taxes are going to press hard enough on the whole of our people. One must realize however, as I already said in English, that we are faced with special conditions arising out of international circumstances beyond our control.
Our own survival is at stake at this time, Mr. Speaker, and it is a question of paying an insurance premium for the survival of
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis our nation, of democracy, and of the freedom we all cherish.
It would have been preferable, I feel, if certain taxes had not been imposed. I must confess, however, that I have not many to suggest other than those I mentioned a moment ago and which I would like, if I may, to repeat in my own tongue.
In my opinion, it would be advisable to consider the possibility of imposing an income tax on certain real estate transactions or on the sale of business establishments because, as I pointed out earlier, I have known of businesses changing hands many times. The sellers were often able to make a profit of $20,000 to $30,000. In the United States there is a tax on such transactions. Perhaps it is too late to include such a measure in this budget. I feel, however, the government should consider the suggestion. It would mean an immediate source of revenue since the tax would be levied at the time these transactions are made. The government would undoubtedly draw substantial revenue which would enable a lowering of the tax on the income of the population in general or at least would allow it to remain at the rate it was before the decision was made to increase it. This is not a clever find I have made. I repeat that it is being done in the United States and I see no reason why it could not be done here also.
The same principle could apply to speculations on the stock market. I have not the time to refute certain arguments that have been advanced against such a step. The matter, however, deserves some consideration from our leaders. In any event, I make this suggestion with a view to alleviating as much as possible the burden which bears too heavily on the working classes and people with smaller means.
Do not think that I would, for one moment, speak or act like a demagogue. Far from it. But someone has to look after the underprivileged and alleviate their burden, if it is not possible to remedy the situation completely.
I am not saying the government failed in its duty in this respect, but one can never do too much and cannot take too great an interest in those people.
The rich, the wealthy and well-to-do can always find a way out of certain financial difficulties, but the underprivileged, abandoned to their lot, are unable to cope with

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis them. I therefore deem it my duty to look after them. Once again, I know that it is the government's intention to alleviate, as much as possible, the burden that crushes those people.
As for the excise taxes being levied-and here I appeal more particularly to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)-I wander whether there is not still time to revise those which are collected on various goods. I do not blame the Minister of Finance, nor do I envy him the task of deciding where to get the revenue he needs; moreover, even if I tried my best, I could never find a popular tax, but I am just making a suggestion. I wonder whether it is still possible to change the tax levied on tobacco, and particularly on leaf tobacco, the kind smoked by poor people.
They cannot afford to treat themselves to a cigar, but these fine Canadians smoke Canadian leaf tobacco which they cut to suit their own taste. Yet, this excise tax may well double the price of leaf tobacco.
I share the views of my colleague from Rimouski (Mr. Rousseau)-although I am no abstainer-that alcoholic beverages should have been taxed instead. People who can afford to have a drink, to use a popular expression, are probably in a position to pay 15 or 20 per cent more or, in any event, enough to enable the Minister of Finance to abolish this excise tax on leaf and cigarette tobacco smoked mostly by people who cannot afford more expensive tobacco or the luxury of a cigar.
The excise tax on chocolate has also been abolished.
I remember that, some years ago, the distributors of soft drinks asked the government to remove the tax on soft drinks, claiming that the popular price was 5 cents, and it was embarrassing to charge a customer
6	cents for a bottle of soft drink, that it was absolutely advisable to return to a price of 5 cents a bottle. What happened? First soft drinks were sold at 6 cents a bottle, then at
7	cents. There you have it. The government did not levy any tax and those who profited thereby were the manufacturers and bottlers who made a profit of more than 40 per cent of the initial price at which they had promised to sell their product.
The same thing occurred in the case of the chocolate bar. We saw it shrink and I am in a position to say so because my son manages a store where these items are sold. The manufacturers wrote to us recently, to tell

us: "No, we will not reduce the price of chocolate bars but we will add a small quantity of chocolate".
I am of the opinion that alcoholic beverages and chocolate bars are not necessities of life and that our good ladies and even gentlemen who enjoy them would gladly sacrifice a bit of chocolate in order to ensure the repeal of certain taxes which, in my humble opinion, are levied too heavily on things which are really necessary to life. I am not, in saying this, censuring the Minister of Finance or, for that matter the present budget, but I do feel that I am duty bound to bring the matter to his attention. Most people in my constituency are really relatively poor-at least they are not particularly well to do. I feel that in making this request I am truly fulfilling my duty towards them.
I have heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) ask our citizens to make sacrifices. Our people are undoubtedly ready to make sacrifices, but there is a limit to everything. We have but one wish: that the international situation, which is the cause of our present financial difficulties, may improve so as to relieve the sufferings of the underprivileged whom, I repeat, it is my duty to defend.
I would have spoken longer but for the rules of the house. However, in concluding my remarks I would like, if I may, to quote from an item published in the March 1951 issue of the Reader's Digest under the signature of Bernard Baruch. I was greatly impressed by this article, which is not at variance with the ideas expressed by the Minister of Finance. I quote:
Today we are being asked to place our own valuation on freedom, in the things we are ready to give up, the taxes we will pay, the selfdiscipline we embrace-in how quickly we will do all this. Let us not haggle, clinging to petty profits and petty comforts. Should we price freedom too low, it will be taken from us.
Unfortunately, when I urged total mobilization of America's military, economic and spiritual resources, there were too many who felt we should "wait and see". They hoped that something would happen to change the attitude of our enemies- those without and those within. Those without are Russia and her satellites. Within are the pressure groups, selfishness, cowardice, inflation, and above all, incompetence in the management of our affairs.
The world is shaping up to a struggle between communism and individualism, between that system which feels the state should be the master and that system, ours, which feels the state should be the servant of the individual.
I warn my fellow Americans that the first battle of the great Armageddon is taking place within our country-now. If our democracy, our government and the institutions founded under its constitution cannot control the conflicting and selfish interests for the over-all welfare, Armageddon will be lost here in our own country. How can our

conscience rest easily when we so unflinchingly send our young men to battle and hesitate to send profits? The situation demands self-denial and sacrifice. Unless we practice these things we shall lose first the spiritual battle of Armageddon and the last will surely be lest-the physical one.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude by expressing the hope that the government will continue to direct their particular attention to the situation which I will not describe as tragic but as very difficult and which now imposes severe hardships upon my constituents. I know that heretofore the government has considered the welfare of this class of people and I hope that our leaders will not miss the opportunity to restore, as soon as possible, the necessary equilibrium in order that each
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis and every one, no matter what social class he may belong to, may in spite of the many difficulties that beset us feel an ever greater happiness in this beautiful country of ours, Canada.
